chunks.x:
DRUG: Ketamine
Class: Dissociative anesthetic / NMDA antagonist
Category: analgesia
Levels: r12, pfc, ccatt
Primary use: Analgesia, procedural sedation, anesthesia induction
Mechanism: Non-competitive NMDA receptor antagonism → dissociative analgesia; sympathomimetic (endogenous catecholamine release → ↑HR, ↑BP); bronchodilation via direct smooth muscle relaxation + catecholamines; anti-inflammatory via NF-κB inhibition at subanesthetic doses; maintains airway reflexes
WARNINGS: Emergence reactions — premedicate with midazolam 0.03 mg/kg. Avoid in penetrating eye injury. NOT truly contraindicated in TBI. Laryngospasm rare but possible. TCCC 2026: co-administration of benzodiazepines with ketamine is NOT recommended; if a casualty is partially dissociated it is safer to give more ketamine than to add a benzodiazepine. Disarm and consider disconnecting communications equipment for casualties given ketamine.
Notes: R1/2 critical insight: if you only have ketamine, you can manage pain AND maintain airway AND temporize hemodynamics. No other single drug does this. TCCC 2026 also lists esketamine 14 or 28mg IN as an equivalent analgesia option for the non-mission-capable casualty.

Ketamine — R12 context: Combat medic cornerstone drug. With ketamine you can: control pain, sedate for procedures, manage bronchospasm, and maintain airway reflexes when intubation is impossible. Single most versatile drug in the R1/2 kit.

Ketamine — PFC context: 18D/IDC standard. Used for RSI (with rocuronium), prolonged field care sedation, TPFC pain management, subanesthetic infusions. Key for austere surgical support and prolonged casualty care.

Ketamine — CCATT context: Full sedation infusion, TIVA component, opioid-sparing protocol. Particularly valuable during CASEVAC where hemodynamic stability is critical and propofol is unavailable or risky.

Ketamine for TCCC 2026 analgesia — non-mission-capable casualty
TCCC 2026: for a casualty who cannot stay in the fight, TCCC medical personnel give ketamine 100mg IM, OR 50mg IN, OR 25mg (or 0.2-0.3 mg/kg) IV/IO over 1 minute. Repeat q30min as needed. Endpoints: reduction of pain or development of nystagmus. For procedural sedation (significant injuries / invasive procedures): 1-2 mg/kg slow IV/IO push, or 300mg (2-3 mg/kg) IM.

Ketamine for Bronchospasm — refractory status asthmaticus
Catecholamine-mediated + direct bronchodilation; induction dose or 0.5 mg/kg/hr infusion for status asthmaticus unresponsive to albuterol. Critical when no nebulizer or albuterol available.

Ketamine for Opioid-sparing analgesia (subanesthetic infusion)
0.1–0.3 mg/kg/hr dramatically reduces morphine/fentanyl requirements; NMDA antagonism blocks central sensitization. Critical when opioids are limited.

Ketamine for Vasopressor-adjunct in distributive shock
Sympathomimetic effect raises BP via catecholamine release — buys time when vasopressors unavailable. NOT for cardiogenic shock.

Ketamine for RSI induction (hemodynamically unstable)
Unlike propofol or etomidate, ketamine maintains or raises BP during RSI in hypovolemic/septic patients. Standard PFC RSI drug.

Ketamine for Combat PTSD / acute stress response (subanesthetic)
0.5 mg/kg IV over 40 min; NMDA antagonism → rapid antidepressant effect; emerging PTSD application.

DRUG: Morphine / Fentanyl
Class: Opioid agonist / μ-receptor agonist
Category: analgesia
Levels: r12, pfc, ccatt
Primary use: [NOT TCCC 2026 TFC first-line analgesia] Moderate-to-severe pain; procedural analgesia; sedation adjunct
Mechanism: μ-opioid receptor agonism → spinal and supraspinal analgesia; reduces sympathetic tone; venodilation (morphine) → preload reduction useful in pulmonary edema; endogenous opioid system modulation; antitussive via medullary cough center suppression
WARNINGS: Respiratory depression — have naloxone ready. Avoid in TBI with hemodynamic instability. Morphine causes histamine release — fentanyl preferred for allergy-prone patients.
Notes: Fentanyl IN (intranasal) is a mission-critical skill: 1.5–2 mcg/kg via MAD atomizer provides analgesia within 5 min without IV access. TCCC 2026 TFC analgesia (Section 11) lists only the CWMP (acetaminophen, meloxicam, suzetrigine) plus ketamine/esketamine as first-line; morphine/fentanyl are not in the TCCC 2026 TFC first-line analgesia list. Opioids retain clinical roles but are a separate clinical-judgment area from the TCCC standard.

Morphine / Fentanyl — R12 context: TCCC pain management. Morphine 5 mg IV/IM or fentanyl 25–50 mcg IV/IN. Battlefield casualty analgesia. Always verify no TBI, no hemodynamic compromise before giving.

Morphine / Fentanyl — PFC context: Full spectrum analgesia including AFAR (oral transmucosal fentanyl citrate), IV PCA concepts in prolonged field care. Fentanyl preferred for rapid onset and titrability.
Morphine / Fentanyl — CCATT context: Continuous opioid infusion for mechanically ventilated casualties. CCATT carries fentanyl infusion standard. Morphine for pulmonary edema/TACO management.

Morphine / Fentanyl for Acute pulmonary edema — venodilation + anxiolysis
Morphine 2–4 mg IV reduces preload via venodilation AND reduces respiratory drive/anxiety; historical use in APE before diuretics take effect.

Morphine / Fentanyl for Intranasal delivery — no IV access (fentanyl)
Fentanyl 1–2 mcg/kg IN via atomizer achieves rapid analgesia with no IV; critical R1/2 capability when IV placement delayed or impossible.

Morphine / Fentanyl for Antitussive for terminal/intubated casualty
Suppresses cough reflex via medullary center; useful for intubated patients during transport to reduce cough-triggered ICP elevation.

k: diarrhea control in prolonged field care
chunks.x:
Morphine / Fentanyl for Diarrhea control in prolonged field care
Opioids slow GI motility; loperamide preferred but morphine can manage severe acute diarrhea impairing mission capability.
chunks.u: Diarrhea control in prolonged field care

chunks.x:
DRUG: Midazolam (Versed)
Class: Benzodiazepine / GABA-A modulator / Amnestic
Category: analgesia
Levels: r12, pfc, ccatt
Primary use: Procedural sedation; seizure control; RSI premedication; anxiolysis
Mechanism: Positive allosteric GABA-A modulator → enhanced Cl⁻ influx → CNS depression, anxiolysis, amnesia, muscle relaxation, anticonvulsant; short-acting benzodiazepine with reliable IV/IM/IN/IO absorption; no analgesic effect
WARNINGS: Respiratory depression when combined with opioids — MUST have airway backup ready. Paradoxical agitation in children and elderly. Do NOT use as sole agent for RSI.
Notes: IM midazolam for status epilepticus is now evidence-based: faster to administer than establishing IV in the field. 10 mg IM for adult SE.

Midazolam (Versed) — R12 context: Seizure control + ketamine premedication. 2.5–5 mg IM/IV for seizures. 0.03 mg/kg IV before ketamine prevents emergence reactions. Intranasal route for seizing patients without IV.
Midazolam (Versed) — PFC context: RSI premedication, sedation adjunct, pharmacological restraint in behavioral emergencies. Buccal/IN route for CASEVAC seizing casualties.
Midazolam (Versed) — CCATT context: ICU sedation infusion component, alcohol/benzo withdrawal management, status epilepticus protocol. Careful dosing in elderly/head-injured.

Midazolam (Versed) for Status epilepticus — first-line IV/IM/IN
5–10 mg IM (faster than IV access) or 0.2 mg/kg IN via atomizer for seizing casualty. IM midazolam is as effective as IV lorazepam for status epilepticus.

k: acute agitation / behavioral emergency — pharmacological restraint
chunks.x:
Midazolam (Versed) for Acute agitation / behavioral emergency — pharmacological restraint
5–10 mg IM + droperidol or haloperidol for acute agitated/combative casualty. Chemical restraint when physical restraint impossible during CASEVAC.
chunks.u: Acute agitation / behavioral emergency — pharmacological restraint

chunks.x:
Midazolam (Versed) for Alcohol/benzodiazepine withdrawal management
Symptom-triggered protocol; midazolam infusion for severe AWS/DTs in prolonged care scenarios.

k: procedural amnesia — no recall of painful procedure
chunks.x:
Midazolam (Versed) for Procedural amnesia — no recall of painful procedure
Amnestic property independent of sedation depth; 1–2 mg IV ensures no memory of painful interventions even when patient appears awake.
chunks.u: Procedural amnesia — no recall of painful procedure

chunks.x:
DRUG: Tranexamic Acid (TXA)
Class: Antifibrinolytic / Lysine analogue
Category: hemostasis
Levels: r12, pfc, ccatt
Primary use: Trauma hemorrhage control; significant TBI; surgical blood loss reduction
Mechanism: Competitive inhibition of plasminogen-to-plasmin conversion → prevents clot dissolution; at pharmacological concentrations also inhibits plasmin-mediated complement activation and kallikrein system → anti-inflammatory + anti-edema secondary effects
WARNINGS: TCCC 2026: give 2g slow IV/IO push as soon as possible but NOT later than 3 hours after injury. Contraindicated in active thromboembolic disease. Note: the prior "1g" dose and "3-hour loading/maintenance split" are superseded by the single 2g push. (Historical context: earlier CRASH-2 subgroup analysis raised concern about late administration; TCCC 2026 frames the 3-hour limit as a cutoff for administration rather than a mortality-increase warning.)
Notes: R1/2 priority drug — ranks with tourniquet and airway management. TCCC 2026 expanded the indication to explicitly include significant TBI and one or more major amputations, and changed dosing to a single 2g IV/IO push. Topical use from crushed tablets remains field-expedient and evidence-supported as an adjunct.

Tranexamic Acid (TXA) — R12 context: TCCC 2026 indication: give if casualty will likely need blood transfusion (hemorrhagic shock, one or more major amputations, penetrating torso trauma, or severe bleeding) OR has signs/symptoms of significant TBI or altered mental status from blast/blunt trauma. Dose: 2g via slow IV or IO push, as soon as possible but not later than 3 hours after injury. Ranks with tourniquet and airway as a top pre-hospital intervention.

Tranexamic Acid (TXA) — PFC context: 2g slow IV/IO push (TCCC 2026 — single dose, no loading/maintenance split). PFC kit also carries TXA for topical wound packing and non-traumatic hemorrhage (e.g. dental bleeding). Give within the 3-hour window.

Tranexamic Acid (TXA) — CCATT context: MTP adjunct. TCCC 2026 specifies a single 2g IV/IO push; the previous 1g loading + 1g infusion protocol is superseded. Monitor for fibrinolysis with TEG/ROTEM when available.

k: hemorrhagic shock / likely transfusion — tccc 2026 primary indication
chunks.x:
Tranexamic Acid (TXA) for Hemorrhagic shock / likely transfusion — TCCC 2026 primary indication
TCCC 2026: 2g via slow IV or IO push as soon as possible, NOT later than 3 hours after injury. Indicated when the casualty will likely need a blood transfusion — hemorrhagic shock, one or more major amputations, penetrating torso trauma, or evidence of severe bleeding.
chunks.u: Hemorrhagic shock / likely transfusion — TCCC 2026 primary indication

chunks.x:
Tranexamic Acid (TXA) for Traumatic amputation — TCCC 2026 indication
One or more major amputations is an explicit TCCC 2026 trigger for TXA (a casualty likely to need transfusion). Give 2g slow IV/IO push within 3 hours of injury, alongside tourniquet hemorrhage control.

k: significant tbi / blast or blunt altered mental status — tccc 2026 indication
chunks.x:
Tranexamic Acid (TXA) for Significant TBI / blast or blunt altered mental status — TCCC 2026 indication
TCCC 2026: if the casualty has signs or symptoms of significant TBI, or altered mental status associated with blast injury or blunt trauma, give 2g slow IV/IO push within 3 hours of injury — even without overt hemorrhage. Supported by CRASH-3 (Lancet 2019, PMID 31623894): TXA within 3h reduces head-injury deaths in mild-moderate TBI.
chunks.u: Significant TBI / blast or blunt altered mental status — TCCC 2026 indication

k: topical hemostasis — wound packing and cavities
chunks.x:
Tranexamic Acid (TXA) for Topical hemostasis — wound packing and cavities
1g TXA in 50 mL NS soaked into gauze or applied topically; achieves high local antifibrinolytic concentration without systemic thrombotic risk. Useful for soft tissue wounds when tourniquet cannot be applied. Topical use is field-expedient (including from crushed tablets) but is an adjunct — not a substitute for the TCCC 2026 systemic 2g indication.
chunks.u: Topical hemostasis — wound packing and cavities

chunks.x:
Tranexamic Acid (TXA) for Epistaxis — topical pledget
TXA-soaked nasal pledget equal or superior to epinephrine-soaked packing; particularly useful in blast injury facial wounds.

Tranexamic Acid (TXA) for Dental/oral hemorrhage in anticoagulated casualty
Crushed tablet or dilute solution as mouthwash; local antifibrinolytic effect without systemic absorption.

Tranexamic Acid (TXA) for Anti-inflammatory — complement and kallikrein inhibition
Plasmin activates complement and kallikrein; TXA by blocking plasmin may reduce edema formation and complement-driven tissue injury in blast wounds.

chunks.x:
DRUG: Calcium (Gluconate / Chloride)
Class: Divalent cation / Cardiac membrane stabilizer / Coagulation cofactor / Antidote (hyperkalemia, CCB OD)
Category: electrolyte
Levels: r12, pfc, ccatt
Primary use: Hyperkalemia cardiac stabilization; massive transfusion citrate toxicity; calcium channel blocker overdose; hydrofluoric acid burns; hypocalcemia
Mechanism: Calcium restores resting membrane potential in hyperkalemia — does NOT lower K+ but stabilizes the cardiac membrane against arrhythmia; CCB OD: competitive antagonism at L-type calcium channels restores cardiac contractility and vascular tone; citrate toxicity: replaces ionized calcium chelated by citrate in stored blood products; HF burns: forms calcium fluoride precipitate, removing fluoride ions; also a cofactor for coagulation factors II, VII, IX, X. Ca gluconate 10% = 0.45 mEq Ca/mL; Ca chloride 10% = 1.36 mEq Ca/mL (~3x more concentrated).
WARNINGS: Calcium CHLORIDE causes severe tissue necrosis with extravasation — central line or large peripheral vein only. Calcium gluconate is safer peripherally. NEVER give calcium IV with sodium bicarbonate (precipitates as calcium carbonate). In digoxin toxicity, calcium administration is CONTROVERSIAL (may worsen dysrhythmias) — proceed with extreme caution.
Notes: Merged entry — previously split across two database records (calcium / calcium_gluconate). Ionized hypocalcemia is the most under-recognized coagulopathy in massive transfusion. TCCC 2026 calcium replacement: 1g (30 mL 10% gluconate or 10 mL 10% chloride) IV/IO after the first transfused product. CaCl vs CaGluc: chloride gives ~3x more ionized calcium per gram — use for life-threatening emergencies; use gluconate for routine replacement and where central access is unavailable.

k: divalent cation / cardiac membrane stabilizer / coagulation cofactor / antidote (hyperkalemia, ccb od)
chunks.x: Calcium (Gluconate / Chloride) — R12 context: Hyperkalemia with ECG changes (peaked T, wide QRS): calcium gluconate 1g IV slow push immediately. Massive transfusion: TCCC 2026 directs 1g calcium (30 mL of 10% calcium gluconate or 10 mL of 10% calcium chloride) IV/IO after the first transfused product. Ionized hypocalcemia is the most under-recognized coagulopathy in massive transfusion.

k: divalent cation / cardiac membrane stabilizer / coagulation cofactor / antidote (hyperkalemia, ccb od)
chunks.x: Calcium (Gluconate / Chloride) — PFC context: Full hyperkalemia protocol. CCB OD (high-dose insulin + calcium protocol). HF acid burns: 2.5% calcium gluconate gel topically or IV/intra-arterial for severe exposures. MTP calcium replacement per TCCC 2026 (after the first transfused product).

k: divalent cation / cardiac membrane stabilizer / coagulation cofactor / antidote (hyperkalemia, ccb od)
chunks.x: Calcium (Gluconate / Chloride) — CCATT context: HDIE (high-dose insulin / epinephrine) protocol for CCB OD. MTP citrate monitoring. Ionized Ca monitoring. CaCl vs CaGluc: calcium chloride preferred for rapid life-threatening situations (central line); calcium gluconate safer peripherally.

k: divalent cation / cardiac membrane stabilizer / coagulation cofactor / antidote (hyperkalemia, ccb od)
massive transfusion citrate toxicity — tccc 2026 calcium replacement
chunks.x:
Calcium (Gluconate / Chloride) for Massive transfusion citrate toxicity — TCCC 2026 calcium replacement
TCCC 2026: if blood products are transfused, administer 1g of calcium (30 mL of 10% calcium gluconate OR 10 mL of 10% calcium chloride) IV/IO after the first transfused product. Citrate in stored blood chelates ionized calcium; hypocalcemia causes reduced cardiac contractility, hypotension, and coagulopathy. (Earlier protocols dosed calcium per ~4 units pRBC or by ionized Ca <1.1 mmol/L; TCCC 2026 simplifies this to 'after the first transfused product'.)
chunks.u: Massive transfusion citrate toxicity — TCCC 2026 calcium replacement

k: divalent cation / cardiac membrane stabilizer / coagulation cofactor / antidote (hyperkalemia, ccb od)
chunks.x:
Calcium (Gluconate / Chloride) for Hyperkalemia — cardiac membrane stabilization (IMMEDIATE)
Calcium gluconate 1g IV over 2-3 min for K+ >6.5 or ECG changes (peaked T waves, wide QRS, sine wave). Effect within 1-3 min, duration 30-60 min. Does NOT lower K+ — buys time for K+ removal. Repeat if the ECG does not normalize.

k: divalent cation / cardiac membrane stabilizer / coagulation cofactor / antidote (hyperkalemia, ccb od)
calcium channel blocker overdose — hdie protocol / membrane rescue
chunks.x:
Calcium (Gluconate / Chloride) for Calcium channel blocker overdose — HDIE protocol / membrane rescue
CCB OD: calcium chloride 1-3g IV bolus (preferred over gluconate for faster effect) + high-dose insulin (1 unit/kg bolus + 0.5-1 unit/kg/hr infusion) + dextrose. Calcium restores contractility and vascular tone at overdosed L-type channels. Critical in CCATT scenarios involving overdose casualties.
chunks.u: Calcium channel blocker overdose — HDIE protocol / membrane rescue

k: divalent cation / cardiac membrane stabilizer / coagulation cofactor / antidote (hyperkalemia, ccb od)
chunks.x:
Calcium (Gluconate / Chloride) for Hydrofluoric acid burns — calcium antidote
HF acid burns: fluoride ions penetrate tissue, bind calcium, and cause hypocalcemia + direct cellular toxicity + pain. Treatment: 2.5% calcium gluconate gel topically (removes fluoride); IV/intra-arterial infusion for hands; systemic hypocalcemia correction. CBRN-relevant.

k: divalent cation / cardiac membrane stabilizer / coagulation cofactor / antidote (hyperkalemia, ccb od)
chunks.x:
Calcium (Gluconate / Chloride) for Hypermagnesemia antidote (tocolytic OD, eclampsia)
1g calcium gluconate IV immediately antagonizes magnesium at the neuromuscular junction and cardiac level; antidote to magnesium toxicity.

DRUG: Hextend / LR / NS
Class: Crystalloid / Colloid resuscitation fluid
Category: hemostasis
Levels: r12, pfc, ccatt
Primary use: Hemorrhagic shock resuscitation; volume expansion
Mechanism: Crystalloids: isotonic sodium-containing solutions restore intravascular volume; Hextend: 6% hetastarch in balanced electrolyte solution → oncotic pressure maintenance + volume expansion (1:1.4 expansion ratio); LR is more physiologic than NS (lower chloride → less hyperchloremic acidosis)
WARNINGS: Excessive crystalloid worsens coagulopathy, hypothermia, and abdominal compartment syndrome. TCCC standard: blood products FIRST, crystalloid only as bridge. Hextend max 1.5L (coagulopathy risk).
Notes: Damage control resuscitation principle: each liter of crystalloid instead of blood dilutes clotting factors. The goal is 1:1:1 (pRBC:FFP:PLT) or whole blood.

Hextend / LR / NS — R12 context: Minimal crystalloid is the TCCC standard — blood products preferred. If no blood available: Hextend 500 mL as damage control resuscitation bridge. Avoid NS >1L (hyperchloremic acidosis worsens coagulopathy).
Hextend / LR / NS — PFC context: PFC (Prolonged Field Care): LR for maintenance, Hextend for volume expansion. 1:1:1 balanced resuscitation with available blood products is the goal.

Hextend / LR / NS — CCATT context: Damage control resuscitation during CASEVAC: permissive hypotension (MAP 50–65 until hemorrhage controlled), minimize crystalloid, maximize blood products. CCATT carries all fluid types.

Hextend / LR / NS for Hypothermia prevention — warmed fluid resuscitation
All IV fluids should be warmed to 42°C for hypothermic casualties; cold crystalloid worsens the lethal triad (hypothermia-acidosis-coagulopathy).

Hextend / LR / NS for Drug dilution vehicle / medication delivery
NS for most drug dilutions; LR incompatible with blood (calcium in LR precipitates citrate-anticoagulated blood). Know your incompatibilities.

k: wound irrigation — ns for open wounds
chunks.x:
Hextend / LR / NS for Wound irrigation — NS for open wounds
NS irrigation of contaminated wounds reduces infection; LR also acceptable; avoid tap water in penetrating wounds if NS available.
chunks.u: Wound irrigation — NS for open wounds

chunks.x:
Hextend / LR / NS for Oral rehydration bridge (LR PO/NGT)
In austere/PFC setting with no IV access and mild-moderate dehydration, LR via nasogastric tube is physiologically sound rehydration.

DRUG: Succinylcholine / Rocuronium
Class: Neuromuscular blocking agents (NMBA)
Category: airway
Levels: pfc, ccatt
Primary use: RSI (Rapid Sequence Intubation) — intubating conditions
Mechanism: Succinylcholine: depolarizing NMB — binds nicotinic ACh receptors persistently → brief fasciculations then paralysis (ultra-short acting 5–10 min); Rocuronium: non-depolarizing NMB — competitive ACh antagonism → paralysis (45–60 min); both require definitive airway management skills
WARNINGS: NEVER give NMBAs without confirmed ability to intubate AND surgical airway backup. Succinylcholine causes fatal hyperkalemia in crush injuries, burns >24h, denervation injuries, prolonged immobilization. Use rocuronium in these patients.
Notes: PFC standard: rocuronium 1.2 mg/kg + ketamine 2 mg/kg = hemodynamically stable RSI. Sugammadex is the safety net — CCATT must carry it.

Succinylcholine / Rocuronium — R12 context: R1/2 does NOT typically carry NMBAs unless specifically trained (18D, PJ, IDC, SOCM). RSI without NMBAs uses ketamine + positioning. Do NOT use NMBAs without intubation proficiency.

Succinylcholine / Rocuronium — PFC context: 18D, IDC (Independent Duty Corpsman), and PJ (Pararescue) carry rocuronium for RSI. Succinylcholine available for some PFC units. Always paired with video laryngoscopy or surgical airway plan.
Succinylcholine / Rocuronium — CCATT context: Full RSI capability. CCATT carries both succinylcholine and rocuronium. Sugammadex carried for rocuronium reversal. Difficult airway algorithm in place.

Succinylcholine / Rocuronium for Laryngospasm rescue — succinylcholine
0.1–0.3 mg/kg IV (subparalyzing dose) breaks laryngospasm without full paralysis; can also use 4 mg/kg IM if no IV access.

Succinylcholine / Rocuronium for Electroconvulsive seizure modification (austere)
Historical use: succinylcholine to prevent musculoskeletal injury during refractory status epilepticus when paralysis is needed for airway protection during seizure management.

Succinylcholine / Rocuronium for Facilitated intubation in non-arrest (rocuronium)
1.2 mg/kg rocuronium provides RSI-equivalent intubating conditions within 60 sec; safer than succinylcholine in crush injury, burns (hyperkalemia risk with succs).

Succinylcholine / Rocuronium for Sugammadex reversal of rocuronium — "undo" paralysis
16 mg/kg sugammadex immediately reverses deep rocuronium paralysis in can't-intubate scenarios. CCATT must carry sugammadex when using rocuronium.

DRUG: Albuterol (Salbutamol)
Class: Short-acting selective β2 agonist (SABA)
Category: airway
Levels: r12, pfc, ccatt
Primary use: Bronchospasm; asthma exacerbation; blast-induced bronchospasm
Mechanism: β2 adrenergic agonism → bronchial smooth muscle relaxation via cAMP-PKA → bronchodilation; activates Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase → K⁺ shift intracellularly; increases mucociliary clearance; uterine relaxation (β2)
WARNINGS: High-dose hyperkalemia protocol causes tachycardia and tremor. NOT definitive K⁺ management — bridge only. Rebound hyperkalemia when effect wears off.
Notes: CRITICAL R1/2 SKILL: High-dose nebulized albuterol (20 mg) for hyperkalemia requires NO IV access. Post-tourniquet release hyperkalemia is a real threat — know this protocol.

Albuterol (Salbutamol) — R12 context: Blast lung injury + bronchospasm is a real combat scenario. MDI + spacer in the IFAK. Also carry nebulizer if available. High-dose albuterol for hyperkalemia is an emergency skill.
Albuterol (Salbutamol) — PFC context: MDI + nebulizer. High-dose protocol for hyperkalemia in PFC. Tocolysis for combat-zone obstetric emergencies.
Albuterol (Salbutamol) — CCATT context: Nebulized + IV if available. High-dose hyperkalemia protocol during CASEVAC when dialysis not possible. Ventilator bronchodilator delivery.

k: hyperkalemia — emergency k⁺ redistribution (no iv needed)
chunks.x:
Albuterol (Salbutamol) for Hyperkalemia — emergency K⁺ redistribution (NO IV needed)
10–20 mg nebulized albuterol (5–10× bronchodilator dose) → Na-K-ATPase activation → K⁺ shifts intracellularly. Lowers K⁺ 0.5–1.5 mEq/L within 30 min. CRITICAL: no IV access needed. Additive to insulin.
chunks.u: Hyperkalemia — emergency K⁺ redistribution (NO IV needed)

chunks.x:
Albuterol (Salbutamol) for Crush injury / rhabdomyolysis hyperkalemia bridge
Post-tourniquet release or crush injury → massive K⁺ release → potentially lethal hyperkalemia. Albuterol buys time when no IV access or no insulin available.

k: blast lung — bronchospasm from pulmonary contusion
chunks.x:
Albuterol (Salbutamol) for Blast lung — bronchospasm from pulmonary contusion
Blast overpressure causes airway reactivity and bronchospasm. Albuterol is first-line for blast lung bronchospasm.
chunks.u: Blast lung — bronchospasm from pulmonary contusion

chunks.x:
Albuterol (Salbutamol) for Mucociliary clearance — smoke inhalation
Increases ciliary beat frequency; assists secretion mobilization in smoke inhalation injury (also from burn casualties in MASCAL).

chunks.x:
DRUG: Sodium Bicarbonate (NaHCO3)
Class: Alkalinizing agent / Buffer / Na⁺ channel rescue agent / Antidote for TCA OD and Na channel blockade
Category: electrolyte
Levels: r12, pfc, ccatt
Primary use: Tricyclic antidepressant overdose; sodium channel blocker toxicity; metabolic acidosis; hyperkalemia adjunct; urinary alkalinization; severe aspirin OD
Mechanism: HCO₃⁻ + H⁺ → CO₂ + H₂O → systemic alkalinization; raises blood pH → competitive displacement of TCA from sodium channels → reverses cardiotoxicity; increases protein binding of weak-acid drugs (TCA, salicylates, cocaine) → reduces free drug toxicity; Na⁺ loading rescues blocked Na⁺ channels and overcomes channel blockade; urinary alkalinization traps ionized salicylate in urine → enhanced elimination; hyperkalemia: alkalinization promotes cellular K⁺ uptake
WARNINGS: TCA OD: QRS >100 ms → bicarbonate NOW, regardless of pH. Do NOT delay for blood gas result. Incompatible with calcium — NEVER mix with calcium-containing solutions (precipitates). Hypernatremia and hyperosmolarity/hypertonicity with excess dosing. Paradoxical intracellular acidosis (CO2 produced crosses cell membrane). Do NOT use for routine metabolic acidosis management in sepsis (no outcome benefit).
Notes: TCA OD reflexive skill: QRS >100 ms after tricyclic ingestion → 1–2 mEq/kg bicarbonate immediately, then infusion to maintain pH 7.45–7.55. Continuous ECG monitoring — QRS should narrow within minutes of appropriate dosing. This can be life-saving before CCATT level care is available.

DRUG: Naloxone (Narcan)
Class: Pure competitive opioid antagonist (μ, κ, δ) / TLR4 antagonist
Category: antidote
Levels: r12, pfc, ccatt
Primary use: Opioid overdose reversal; respiratory depression from battlefield opioid use; post-anesthesia reversal
Mechanism: Competitive antagonism at mu, kappa, and delta opioid receptors → reverses all opioid effects including analgesia, sedation, respiratory depression, miosis, GI effects; onset IV 2 min, IM 5 min, IN 5-10 min; half-life 30-80 min (SHORTER than most opioids — re-narcotization possible); dose-dependent reversal: low dose (0.04 mg) reverses respiratory depression without precipitating full withdrawal; infusion for prolonged opioid OD; non-opioid pathway: TLR4 antagonism → anti-neuroinflammatory at ultra-low doses
WARNINGS: SHORT HALF-LIFE (30-80 min) — SHORTER than most opioids. Re-sedation is EXPECTED; the casualty can re-narcotize after apparent recovery. Plan for repeat dosing every 30–60 min or infusion during transport, and monitor for a minimum of 4-6 h after reversal. Do not leave a reversed casualty unmonitored. Precipitates acute opioid withdrawal in dependent patients — use titrated dosing. High doses in opioid-dependent patients → agitation, vomiting, pulmonary edema, cardiac dysrhythmias.
Notes: Intranasal 2–4 mg is now the standard pre-hospital route — no IV needed. Field naloxone: IN delivery 2 mg via MAD or IM 0.4-2 mg. TCCC opioid protocol: ketamine preferred for pain management to reduce opioid use; when opioids are used, naloxone must be immediately available. CCATT critical skill: naloxone infusion during CASEVAC for long-acting opioid OD. Re-narcotization monitoring is mandatory — the reversal is not the end of care.

DRUG: Vasopressin
Class: Endogenous nonapeptide / V1 / V2 receptor agonist / Endogenous peptide hormone / V1 vasopressor / V2 antidiuretic / GI vasoconstrictor
Category: vasoactive
Levels: pfc, ccatt
Primary use: Refractory vasodilatory shock; catecholamine-sparing; cardiac arrest. Distributive shock vasopressor; cardiac arrest; variceal hemorrhage; diabetes insipidus; refractory hemorrhagic shock adjunct
Mechanism: V1 receptor → vascular smooth muscle contraction INDEPENDENT of catecholamine receptors; V2 → renal water reabsorption (ADH); effective when catecholamine receptors downregulated by prolonged shock or acidosis; vasopressin is depleted in septic shock. V1 receptor agonism → peripheral vasoconstriction (catecholamine-independent); V2 receptor agonism → renal water reabsorption (ADH effect); V1 in GI tract → splanchnic vasoconstriction → reduces portal pressure for variceal bleeding; depleted in prolonged septic shock → exogenous replacement restores vascular tone
WARNINGS: Do not exceed 0.04 U/min in septic shock — mesenteric and digital ischemia. Not a first-line vasopressor — always combine with or add to norepinephrine. Coronary vasoconstriction — use with caution in known CAD. Mesenteric ischemia with high doses. Hyponatremia with excessive V2 stimulation. Not titratable like norepinephrine for BP management alone.
Notes: Key tactical teaching: vasopressin is the "backup" vasopressor when catecholamine receptors are exhausted. Prolongs survival in prolonged shock when NE alone is failing. DI after TBI or pituitary surgery: urine output >250 mL/hr + rising serum sodium = central DI. Desmopressin 1-4 mcg IV/SQ preferred over vasopressin for DI (pure V2 effect, no hemodynamic changes).
Vasopressin — PFC context: PFC vasopressor option when norepinephrine/epinephrine depleted or patient has downregulated catecholamine receptors after prolonged shock. 0.03–0.04 U/min.
Vasopressin — CCATT context: Standard second vasopressor in septic shock (add at NE >0.25 mcg/kg/min). Central DI management after TBI. Variceal bleeding bridge.

Vasopressin for Catecholamine-refractory shock — receptor-independent vasoconstriction
When NE/epi receptors downregulated after prolonged shock or acidosis, vasopressin via V1 remains effective. This is the key mechanistic insight.

Vasopressin for Central diabetes insipidus — ADH replacement
TBI frequently causes central DI; vasopressin V2 agonism provides ADH effect; manages hypernatremia during CASEVAC when DDAVP unavailable.

Vasopressin for Variceal hemorrhage — portal pressure reduction
Splanchnic V1 vasoconstriction reduces portal pressure; bridge to endoscopy/TIPS. Relevant in combat or deployed hospital settings.

DRUG: Amiodarone
Class: Class III antiarrhythmic / Multi-channel blocker
Category: cardiac

Mechanism: Blocks K⁺ (IKr), Na⁺, Ca²⁺ channels AND β-adrenergic receptors → prolongs action potential duration in all cardiac tissue; rich iodine content (39% by weight) → Wolff-Chaikoff thyroid inhibition; widest spectrum of any antiarrhythmic
WARNINGS: QT prolongation — avoid with other QT-prolonging drugs. Hypotension with IV loading. Long-term: pulmonary toxicity, thyroid dysfunction, hepatotoxicity (not relevant for acute use).
Notes: For acute/CASEVAC use, risk-benefit clearly favorable. The thyroid storm use is an elegant emergency application of the Wolff-Chaikoff effect.
Amiodarone — PFC context: Cardiac arrest VF/VT protocol. 300 mg IV push in refractory VF after 3 shocks. PFC providers with ACLS capability carry amiodarone.
Amiodarone — CCATT context: Full antiarrhythmic protocol. Chemical cardioversion of AF during transport. VT suppression in myocarditis/trauma. Thyroid storm adjunct.

DRUG: Atropine
Class: Anticholinergic / Muscarinic antagonist
Category: cardiac
Levels: r12, pfc, ccatt
Primary use: Symptomatic bradycardia; nerve agent antidote (MARK1); airway secretions
Mechanism: Competitive muscarinic (M1–M5) antagonist → blocks vagal tone on heart (→ ↑HR), blocks GI motility, reduces glandular secretions, causes bronchodilation, mydriasis, urinary retention; crosses BBB → CNS effects at high doses; antidote for organophosphate-excess muscarinic stimulation
WARNINGS: Do not use for infranodal (wide complex) bradycardia — may worsen. In organophosphate poisoning: may need massive doses (20–100 mg in severe cases). Never withhold atropine in nerve agent OD for fear of overdose.

Atropine — R12 context: CBRN MARK1 autoinjector for nerve agent exposure (paired with 2-PAM). Also first-line for symptomatic bradycardia. Every IFAK in CBRN-threat environments.
Atropine — PFC context: Full CBRN kit: atropine + pralidoxime (2-PAM). Pre-treatment with pyridostigmine for potential nerve agent exposure. Airway secretion management.
Atropine — CCATT context: Full ACLS bradycardia protocol. Organophosphate toxidrome management. Post-intubation secretion management. Anticholinergic bronchodilation.

DRUG: Dexamethasone
Class: Synthetic glucocorticoid / NF-κB inhibitor / Anti-edema
Category: antiinflam
Levels: r12, pfc, ccatt

chunks.x:
DRUG: Doxycycline
Class: Tetracycline antibiotic / MMP inhibitor / CBRN agent / Protein synthesis inhibitor / Intracellular pathogen coverage
Category: abx
Levels: r12, pfc, ccatt
Primary use: Atypical pneumonia; CBRN (anthrax, plague, tularemia, brucellosis); STIs; malaria prophylaxis. Malaria prophylaxis; anthrax treatment/PEP; Rickettsial diseases; RMSF; Lyme disease; CAP; SSTI; STIs; anti-inflammatory (subantimicrobial dose)
Mechanism: 30S ribosomal inhibitor → bacteriostatic broad spectrum; intracellular penetration (Rickettsia, Chlamydia, Brucella); MMP (matrix metalloproteinase) inhibition at sub-antimicrobial doses → anti-inflammatory and anti-collagenolytic; anti-collagenase in wound healing. Inhibits 30S ribosomal subunit → blocks aminoacyl-tRNA binding → bacteriostatic; excellent intracellular penetration → effective for obligate intracellular pathogens (Rickettsia, Chlamydia, Brucella, Q fever); oral bioavailability 93%; long half-life (18-22h) → once or twice daily dosing; anti-inflammatory at subantimicrobial doses via MMP inhibition
WARNINGS: Photosensitivity — critical in desert/tropical deployments. Take with food; esophageal ulceration without adequate water. Avoid in pregnancy and children <8 years (teeth staining, bone growth). Photosensitivity — severe sunburn risk in deployed tropical sun; use sunscreen. Esophageal irritation — take with full glass of water and remain upright 30 min. Take 2h before or 6h after calcium/antacids (chelation reduces absorption). Tooth discoloration historical concern with prolonged pediatric use.
Notes: CBRN critical drug: doxycycline is the only antibiotic that covers BOTH bacterial CBRN agents (anthrax, plague, tularemia) AND Rickettsia/intracellular tick-borne fevers. Cannot be fully replaced. RMSF teaching: doxycycline is safe in ALL ages for RMSF (including children <8 years when life-threatening) — the benefit far outweighs cosmetic tooth risk. Do NOT use alternative antibiotics for suspected RMSF — chloramphenicol is the only alternative and is inferior. Empiric treatment saves lives.

DRUG: Ciprofloxacin
Class: Fluoroquinolone / DNA gyrase / Topoisomerase IV inhibitor
Category: abx
Levels: r12, pfc, ccatt
Primary use: Gram-negative infections; UTI; GI infections; CBRN post-exposure prophylaxis. Anthrax post-exposure prophylaxis; plague treatment; traveler diarrhea; UTI; Pseudomonas; bioterrorism agent treatment
Mechanism: Inhibits bacterial DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV → prevents DNA supercoiling → bactericidal; broad gram-negative + some gram-positive + atypical coverage; excellent intracellular penetration; near 100% oral bioavailability (IV = PO in efficacy). Inhibits bacterial DNA gyrase (gram-negative focus) and topoisomerase IV → prevents DNA supercoiling and replication → bactericidal; broad gram-negative spectrum including Pseudomonas; excellent oral bioavailability (~80%) = IV equivalent; penetrates intracellular environments — effective for intracellular pathogens; active against Bacillus anthracis and Yersinia pestis
WARNINGS: Tendon rupture (especially Achilles) — particularly with steroids. Avoid in children, pregnant. QT prolongation. Increasing fluoroquinolone resistance globally. Tendinopathy and tendon rupture (especially Achilles in >60 years or steroid users). QTc prolongation. Doubles theophylline and caffeine levels (drug interaction). Peripheral neuropathy. Avoid in growing children (<18) except life-threatening indications (anthrax). Fluoroquinolone-resistant gram-negatives increasing.
Notes: Near 100% oral bioavailability means ciprofloxacin PO is equivalent to IV for systemic infections — critical in field/PFC settings where IV access is limited. Anthrax PEP teaching: 60-day course required because anthrax spores can germinate late in alveolar macrophages. Shorter courses fail. DRUG: Norepinephrine (Levophed)
Class: Endogenous catecholamine / α1, β1 agonist / Alpha-1 dominant + Beta-1 agonist / First-line vasopressor
Category: vasoactive
Levels: pfc, ccatt
Primary use: First-line vasopressor for septic and distributive shock. Septic shock first-line vasopressor; distributive shock; post-cardiac arrest MAP support; refractory hypotension
Mechanism: Potent α1 agonism → ↑SVR (vasoconstriction); moderate β1 → inotropy without significant tachycardia; minimal β2; most evidence-based vasopressor for septic shock per Surviving Sepsis guidelines. Alpha-1 dominant agonism → potent peripheral vasoconstriction → increases SVR and MAP; beta-1 agonism → mild inotropy/chronotropy; maintains coronary and cerebral perfusion pressure; superior to dopamine for septic shock mortality (SOAP II trial); central line preferred but peripheral acceptable temporarily
WARNINGS: Central line REQUIRED — extravasation causes tissue necrosis. Phentolamine for extravasation rescue. Tissue necrosis with extravasation — treat immediately with phentolamine 5 mg in 10 mL NS infiltrated into area. Reflex bradycardia at high doses. Mesenteric ischemia with prolonged high-dose use. Peripheral IV: monitor every 30 min for extravasation.
Notes: CCATT carries NE as primary vasopressor for CASEVAC. Full hemodynamic monitoring (A-line, CVP) ideal during transport. NE extravasation antidote: phentolamine 5-10 mg in 10 mL NS injected into extravasated area within 12h reverses necrosis. Every provider using peripheral NE must know this — prevention and treatment.

Norepinephrine (Levophed) — CCATT context: CCATT standard vasopressor. Infusion during transport. Central line required. Full hemodynamic monitoring during CASEVAC. Septic shock, post-arrest support, neurogenic shock.

Norepinephrine (Levophed) for Neurogenic / spinal shock
Loss of sympathetic tone from SCI → profound vasodilation; NE restores SVR without excessive tachycardia; critical for SCI casualties during CASEVAC.

Norepinephrine (Levophed) for Post-ROSC hemodynamic support
Target MAP >65 post-ROSC; NE maintains coronary and cerebral perfusion pressure during transport.

Norepinephrine (Levophed) for Hepatorenal syndrome vasopressor adjunct
Systemic vasoconstriction offsets splanchnic vasodilation driving HRS; combined with albumin for HRS-AKI.

DRUG: Heparin / Enoxaparin (LMWH)
Class: Anticoagulant / Antithrombin III activator
Category: hemostasis
Levels: ccatt
Primary use: DVT/PE treatment and prevention; ACS anticoagulation; circuit anticoagulation (ECMO, CRRT)
Mechanism: Activates antithrombin III → inhibits thrombin (IIa) and Factor Xa; heparin (UFH) has additional antithrombin direct effect; anticoagulates both forming and existing clots; rapid onset/offset with UFH; enoxaparin (LMWH) more predictable, renal clearance
WARNINGS: Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia (HIT) — monitor platelets. Reversal: Protamine 1 mg per 100 units UFH. LMWH partially reversed by protamine (60%). Avoid in active hemorrhage.
Notes: CCATT must balance anticoagulation for ACS/DVT/circuit patency against hemorrhage risk in polytrauma. UFH preferred for titrability and protamine reversibility during transport.

Heparin / Enoxaparin (LMWH) — CCATT context: DVT prophylaxis during prolonged CASEVAC. PE treatment in transit. ACS anticoagulation. ECMO/CRRT circuit anticoagulation. Critical in polytrauma where clotting and bleeding coexist.

Heparin / Enoxaparin (LMWH) for CASEVAC DVT prophylaxis — immobilized casualty
Enoxaparin 40 mg SQ daily; critically ill immobilized casualties during prolonged transport develop DVT rapidly. CCATT initiates prophylaxis.

Heparin / Enoxaparin (LMWH) for ACS/NSTEMI anticoagulation during transport
UFH 60 units/kg IV bolus then infusion; CCATT manages ACS casualties requiring anticoagulation during CASEVAC to cardiac catheterization.

Heparin / Enoxaparin (LMWH) for ECMO/CRRT circuit anticoagulation
UFH continuous infusion to maintain ECMO/CRRT circuit patency; titrated to anti-Xa or aPTT.

Heparin / Enoxaparin (LMWH) for Catheter line flush and lock
Heparin-saline (10–100 units/mL) for CVC and arterial line lock; prevents thrombosis in indwelling catheters during transport.

DRUG: Propofol
Class: Alkylphenol IV anesthetic / GABA-A modulator
Category: analgesia
Levels: ccatt
Primary use: ICU sedation; CASEVAC sedation; anesthesia induction
Mechanism: Positive allosteric GABA-A modulator → CNS depression; anti-emetic via D2/5-HT3 antagonism; antioxidant phenol moiety; lipid emulsion vehicle; short context-sensitive half-time
WARNINGS: PROPOFOL INFUSION SYNDROME (PRIS): >4 mg/kg/hr >48h → rhabdomyolysis, acidosis, cardiac failure. Monitor triglycerides. Lipid emulsion — infection control essential.
Notes: CCATT PRIS protocol: if rate >4 mg/kg/hr needed, switch to ketamine+midazolam after 48h. Monitor CK, triglycerides, lactate.
Propofol — CCATT context: Standard CCATT sedation during mechanically ventilated CASEVAC. RASS −2 to 0 target during transport. PRIS monitoring mandatory >4 mg/kg/hr.

Propofol for Status epilepticus — GABA-A rescue
1–2 mg/kg IV bolus terminates refractory SE; then infusion. GABA-A mechanism distinguishes from Na+ channel drugs.

Propofol for Rescue antiemetic (subhypnotic)
10–20 mg IV subhypnotic bolus; D2/5-HT3 antagonism provides antiemetic effect independently of sedation. For refractory PONV during CASEVAC.

Propofol for ICP reduction — burst suppression
Reduces CMRO2; burst suppression for refractory ICP when barbiturates unavailable.

DRUG: N-Acetylcysteine (NAC)
Class: Antioxidant / GSH precursor / Cytoprotectant
Category: antidote
Levels: pfc, ccatt
Primary use: Acetaminophen OD antidote; mucolytic; antioxidant cytoprotectant
Mechanism: Replenishes intracellular glutathione (GSH) by supplying cysteine; directly scavenges reactive oxygen species (ROS); restores redox balance; anti-inflammatory via NF-κB inhibition. A single GSH/ROS axis underlies acetaminophen-OD protection and the investigational cytoprotective uses (ischemia-reperfusion, oxidative pulmonary injury, neuroprotection).
WARNINGS: IV loading for acetaminophen OD: 150 mg/kg over 60 min → 50 mg/kg over 4h → 100 mg/kg over 16h. Do not delay for acetylcysteine levels if the Rumack-Matthew nomogram indicates treatment. Anaphylactoid reactions can occur with rapid IV infusion (rate-related; slow the infusion). The IRI, TBI, smoke-inhalation, and sepsis uses are investigational/emerging — not TCCC-endorsed and not a substitute for standard care.
Notes: Mechanistic dual-use example — and the paradigm case for TCCC-RX's reasoning approach: one GSH/ROS axis connects the established acetaminophen-OD antidote role to investigational cytoprotection in ischemia-reperfusion injury, oxidative pulmonary injury, and early TBI. The established indication is acetaminophen OD; the extensions are tiered emerging/investigational and src-tagged so they are never read as TCCC recommendations.

N-Acetylcysteine (NAC) — PFC context: Acetaminophen/Tylenol OD is surprisingly common in austere settings — IV loading protocol applies. Investigational antioxidant uses: ischemia-reperfusion injury, smoke inhalation/blast lung, mild TBI. Contrast nephropathy protection.

N-Acetylcysteine (NAC) — CCATT context: Full acetaminophen-OD protocol with hepatotoxicity. Contrast-induced nephropathy prophylaxis. Investigational antioxidant adjunct in IRI, sepsis/MODS, and oxidative pulmonary injury — emerging-grade, not established.

N-Acetylcysteine (NAC) for Acetaminophen overdose — GSH repletion antidote
Established antidote. IV: 150 mg/kg over 60 min → 50 mg/kg over 4h → 100 mg/kg over 16h. Restores hepatic GSH before the oxidative metabolite (NAPQI) causes hepatocellular necrosis. Do not delay for acetylcysteine levels if the Rumack-Matthew nomogram indicates treatment.

N-Acetylcysteine (NAC) for Contrast-induced nephropathy prevention
600–1200 mg PO BID × 2 days peri-procedure; the most cost-effective renal protection before contrast-enhanced CT in a field hospital. Same antioxidant mechanism.

k: mild traumatic brain injury — early antioxidant neuroprotection
chunks.x:
N-Acetylcysteine (NAC) for Mild traumatic brain injury — early antioxidant neuroprotection
Mechanistic dual use: the GSH/ROS axis targets the oxidative component of TBI secondary injury. A double-blind placebo-controlled study in blast mild TBI showed improved symptom resolution with early NAC, and a 2025 RCT in moderate-to-severe TBI reported reductions in oxidative and inflammatory biomarkers (NSE, MDA, S100B, IL-6). A 2026 systematic review identified acute mild TBI as the strongest NAC neurological indication. Evidence is promising but not established; NOT a TCCC recommendation. Dosing regimens vary across studies — no single field-standard dose.

DRUG: OTFC / Oral Fentanyl (Lollipop)
Class: Oral transmucosal fentanyl / μ-opioid agonist
Category: analgesia
Levels: pfc
Primary use: Self-administered battlefield analgesia; rapid-onset opioid delivery without IV

Security implications: wounded operator can remain alert while managing own pain. Note: OTFC is not on the TCCC 2026 TFC first-line analgesia list (CWMP + ketamine/esketamine).

OTFC / Oral Fentanyl (Lollipop) — PFC context: standard kit item. Self/buddy-administered. No IV needed. casualty can self-medicate for extremity injuries without compromising security. 800 mcg unit-dose lollipop.

chunks.x:

OTFC / Oral Fentanyl (Lollipop) for Opioid-sparing multimodal (OTFC + ketamine)

DRUG: Pralidoxime (2-PAM)
Class: Cholinesterase reactivator / Oxime / CBRN antidote
Category: antidote
Levels: r12, pfc, ccatt
Primary use: Organophosphate nerve agent antidote (paired with atropine)
Mechanism: Reactivates acetylcholinesterase inhibited by organophosphate nerve agents BEFORE "aging" (irreversible binding) occurs; restores cholinesterase function; effective at nicotinic sites (muscle weakness) where atropine has no effect; must be given within minutes to hours of exposure
WARNINGS: TIME IS CRITICAL — aging (irreversible OP-cholinesterase binding) begins within minutes for some agents (soman = very fast aging). Give 2-PAM IMMEDIATELY with atropine. After aging, 2-PAM is ineffective.
Notes: CBRN teaching: atropine + 2-PAM together. Atropine alone keeps the patient alive by blocking muscarinic effects. 2-PAM actually fixes the cholinesterase. Both required.
Pralidoxime (2-PAM) — R12 context: MARK1 autoinjector kit (atropine + 2-PAM-Cl). Battlefield CBRN standard. Two MARK1 kits per soldier in high-threat environments. Buddy aid protocol.

Pralidoxime (2-PAM) — PFC context: Full CBRN kit. Multiple 2-PAM doses available. Know: atropine treats muscarinic effects (secretions, bradycardia, bronchospasm); 2-PAM reactivates cholinesterase (restores all effects including nicotinic weakness).
Pralidoxime (2-PAM) — CCATT context: Hospital CBRN protocol. 2-PAM infusion for severe OP poisoning after MARK1 doses. Support toxidrome management.

Pralidoxime (2-PAM) for Pesticide (organophosphate) poisoning — civilian CBRN
Identical mechanism to nerve agents; 2-PAM + atropine for agricultural OP pesticide poisoning (common in deployment areas).

Pralidoxime (2-PAM) for Combined nicotinic + muscarinic reversal
Atropine covers muscarinic (secretions, bronchospasm, bradycardia); ONLY 2-PAM reverses nicotinic weakness (paralysis, respiratory failure). Both drugs required for full reversal.
