Primary use: Moderate-severe acute pain; opioid-sparing; JTS CPG multimodal analgesia
Mechanism: Inhibits COX-1 and COX-2 → reduces prostaglandin and thromboxane synthesis → analgesia + anti-inflammatory; ureteral smooth muscle relaxation; inhibits platelet thromboxane A2 → antiplatelet effect
WARNINGS: MAXIMUM 5 DAYS. CONTRAINDICATED in hemorrhagic casualties, suspected internal bleeding, dehydration, AKI. Platelet inhibition lasts 24-48h after stopping.
Notes: JTS CAUTION: contraindicated in penetrating torso trauma until hemorrhage definitively controlled. Safe for isolated extremity injuries after hemostasis achieved.

Ketorolac (Toradol) — R12 context: JTS CPG: 15-30 mg IM for moderate pain. CAUTION: do NOT use in suspected internal hemorrhage or hemorrhagic shock. Safe for isolated extremity injuries after hemorrhage controlled.
Ketorolac (Toradol) — PFC context: Part of multimodal analgesia triad with acetaminophen + ketamine. 30 mg IM/IV; limit to 5 days. Useful for musculoskeletal injuries, dental pain, renal colic.
Ketorolac (Toradol) — CCATT context: IV 15-30 mg q6h; monitor renal function during CASEVAC. Stop if creatinine rising.

k: renal colic — ureteral smooth muscle relaxation
chunks.x:
Ketorolac (Toradol) for Renal colic — ureteral smooth muscle relaxation
Prostaglandin inhibition reduces ureteral tone; comparable to opioid analgesia for ureteric colic; 30 mg IV/IM. Mission-critical for deployed urologic emergencies.
chunks.u: Renal colic — ureteral smooth muscle relaxation

chunks.x:
Ketorolac (Toradol) for Migraine — emergency abortive therapy
IV ketorolac 30 mg as effective as opioids for migraine in emergency settings.

Ketorolac (Toradol) for Post-op opioid reduction 25-50%
Perioperative ketorolac significantly reduces opioid consumption; effective for orthopedic and abdominal procedures.

Ketorolac (Toradol) for Pericarditis — anti-inflammatory
NSAID backbone of pericarditis treatment; reduces pericardial inflammation.

DRUG: Meloxicam (Mobic)
Class: Preferential COX-2 inhibitor / NSAID
Category: analgesia
Levels: r12, pfc
Primary use: TCCC 2026 CWMP component; Mild-moderate musculoskeletal pain; JTS CPG Step 1 analgesia
Mechanism: Preferential COX-2 inhibition (10:1 COX-2:COX-1 selectivity) → reduced prostaglandin synthesis; less COX-1 inhibition = less GI toxicity and less platelet inhibition than non-selective NSAIDs; long half-life (20h) → once daily dosing
WARNINGS: Still has some platelet inhibition — avoid in active hemorrhage. GI risk less than ibuprofen but not zero. Renal vasoconstriction possible in dehydration.
Notes: JTS Pain CPG preferred PO NSAID for combat setting: meloxicam 15 mg daily is simpler than ibuprofen TID and has less platelet effect.

Meloxicam (Mobic) — R12 context: JTS Pain CPG Step 1 mild pain: meloxicam 15 mg PO daily. Preferred PO NSAID for combat casualties — once daily dosing, less platelet effect than ibuprofen. Soldier self-carry item.
Meloxicam (Mobic) — PFC context: PFC mild-moderate musculoskeletal pain management. Combine with acetaminophen for additive effect without increasing platelet risk.

Meloxicam (Mobic) for CWMP analgesia — TCCC 2026 mission-capable casualty
TCCC 2026 Combat Wound Medication Pack: meloxicam 15 mg PO once daily. Given alongside acetaminophen 1000-1300 mg PO q8h and suzetrigine for a casualty who can stay in the fight.

k: jts step 1 analgesia — mild combat pain
chunks.x:
Meloxicam (Mobic) for JTS Step 1 analgesia — mild combat pain
JTS Pain CPG first-line for mild pain: meloxicam 15 mg PO daily. Preferred over ibuprofen due to once-daily dosing and reduced platelet inhibition.
chunks.u: JTS Step 1 analgesia — mild combat pain

chunks.x:
Meloxicam (Mobic) for Musculoskeletal injury management
Sprains, strains, fractures — anti-inflammatory + analgesic; allows mission continuation for mild injuries.

k: chronic pain management in prolonged field care
chunks.x:
Meloxicam (Mobic) for Chronic pain management in prolonged field care
Once-daily dosing simplifies PFC pain protocol; less GI risk with longer use than non-selective NSAIDs.
chunks.u: Chronic pain management in prolonged field care

chunks.x:
DRUG: Ondansetron (Zofran)
Class: Selective 5-HT3 receptor antagonist / Antiemetic
Category: analgesia
Levels: r12, pfc, ccatt
Primary use: Nausea and vomiting; opioid-induced nausea; post-op nausea
Mechanism: Selective 5-HT3 antagonism in GI tract and CNS → blocks vagal afferent stimulation of vomiting center; no dopamine antagonism → no extrapyramidal side effects; no sedation; safe in TBI
WARNINGS: QT prolongation at high doses — avoid with other QT-prolonging drugs. Serotonin syndrome risk with concurrent serotonergic drugs (rare at standard doses). ODT dissolves in 30 seconds sublingually.
Notes: ODT (orally disintegrating tablet) form is tactically ideal — no water, works even in vomiting patient. Standard in JTS pain management CPG as antiemetic adjunct.

Ondansetron (Zofran) — R12 context: JTS CPG: ondansetron 4 mg ODT (orally disintegrating tablet) or IV/IM for nausea. Dissolves under tongue — no water needed. Critical for opioid-induced nausea in casualties.
Ondansetron (Zofran) — PFC context: ODT form ideal for tactical use. IV/IM for severe nausea. Antiemetic for CASEVAC motion sickness and opioid nausea.
Ondansetron (Zofran) — CCATT context: IV 4-8 mg q6-8h. Standard antiemetic during transport. Combine with dexamethasone for PONV prevention.

k: opioid-induced nausea — enables opioid analgesia compliance
chunks.x:
Ondansetron (Zofran) for Opioid-induced nausea — enables opioid analgesia compliance
Uncontrolled nausea leads to opioid refusal in conscious casualties; ondansetron enables therapeutic opioid use.
chunks.u: Opioid-induced nausea — enables opioid analgesia compliance

chunks.x:
Ondansetron (Zofran) for CASEVAC motion sickness
5-HT3 antagonism reduces vestibular-triggered nausea during helicopter/aircraft transport.

Ondansetron (Zofran) for Chemotherapy/radiation nausea
Original indication; highly effective for emetogenic therapy.

Ondansetron (Zofran) for Itch (pruritus) from opioids — adjunct
5-HT3 antagonism reduces opioid-induced pruritus; alternative to low-dose naloxone.

k: vitamin b12 analogue / cyanide antidote / nitric oxide scavenger
chunks.x:
DRUG: Hydroxocobalamin (Cyanokit)
Class: Vitamin B12 analogue / Cyanide antidote / Nitric oxide scavenger
Category: antidote
Levels: pfc, ccatt
Primary use: Cyanide poisoning antidote; smoke inhalation CN toxicity; CBRN; investigational vasoplegia rescue
Mechanism: Binds CN⁻ with affinity exceeding cytochrome c oxidase → forms renally-excreted cyanocobalamin (vitamin B12). Independently scavenges nitric oxide (NO) and binds hydrogen sulfide (H₂S) → reduces NO/H₂S-mediated vasodilation, raising vascular tone. Methemoglobin-independent — safe in CO co-poisoning, unlike nitrite-based antidotes. The same NO-scavenging mechanism that contributes to the cyanide toxidrome response also underlies its investigational use in vasoplegic shock.
WARNINGS: Turns skin/urine RED for 2-5 days — warn patient and staff. Incompatible with sodium thiosulfate in same IV line. Do NOT delay for CN blood levels — treat empirically in smoke inhalation. Vasoplegia use is investigational and not TCCC-endorsed: it does not replace standard fluid resuscitation and first-line vasopressors.
Notes: KEY ADVANTAGE over nitrite antidotes: safe with CO co-poisoning — structure fires always produce both CN and CO. Mechanistic dual-use example: NO scavenging links the cyanide-antidote role to investigational vasoplegia rescue. The vasoplegia indication is actively studied (2023 systematic review, multiple case series) but remains observational-grade — labeled emerging/investigational and src-tagged accordingly.

k: vitamin b12 analogue / cyanide antidote / nitric oxide scavenger
chunks.x: Hydroxocobalamin (Cyanokit) — PFC context: CBRN CN antidote. 5g IV over 15 min. Smoke inhalation in structure fires, industrial CN exposure, mass casualty chemical events. Safe with concurrent CO poisoning — critical advantage over sodium nitrite.

k: vitamin b12 analogue / cyanide antidote / nitric oxide scavenger
chunks.x: Hydroxocobalamin (Cyanokit) — CCATT context: Full CN toxidrome management. 5g IV bolus; repeat 5g if inadequate response (up to 15g total). Superior to sodium thiosulfate alone for acute severe CN poisoning. May also be encountered as a rescue agent for catecholamine-refractory vasoplegia (investigational — see dual uses).

k: smoke inhalation — cn + co combined poisoning
vitamin b12 analogue / cyanide antidote / nitric oxide scavenger
chunks.x:
Hydroxocobalamin (Cyanokit) for Smoke inhalation — CN + CO combined poisoning
Structure fires produce both HCN and CO. Hydroxocobalamin is the ONLY CN antidote safe with concurrent CO poisoning — nitrites form methemoglobin which worsens CO toxicity. 5g IV over 15 min. Critical for fire casualty CBRN management.
chunks.u: Smoke inhalation — CN + CO combined poisoning

k: vitamin b12 analogue / cyanide antidote / nitric oxide scavenger
chunks.x:
Hydroxocobalamin (Cyanokit) for CBRN mass casualty CN exposure
Weaponized hydrogen cyanide (AC) or cyanogen chloride (CK) exposure. 5g IV rapidly reverses CN-induced cellular hypoxia. Repeat 5g for severe/persistent toxicity.

k: unexplained lactic acidosis — empiric cn antidote
vitamin b12 analogue / cyanide antidote / nitric oxide scavenger
chunks.x:
Hydroxocobalamin (Cyanokit) for Unexplained lactic acidosis — empiric CN antidote
In smoke inhalation or industrial exposure with unexplained lactic acidosis and hemodynamic instability, empiric hydroxocobalamin is justified even without a confirmed CN level.
chunks.u: Unexplained lactic acidosis — empiric CN antidote

k: refractory vasoplegic / distributive shock — no scavenging rescue (investigational)
vitamin b12 analogue / cyanide antidote / nitric oxide scavenger
chunks.x:
Hydroxocobalamin (Cyanokit) for Refractory vasoplegic / distributive shock — NO scavenging rescue (investigational)
Mechanistic dual use: the same NO-scavenging action relevant to CN toxidrome physiology raises vascular tone in catecholamine-refractory vasodilatory shock. Reported 5g IV bolus over 10-15 min. Evidence is limited to case reports, case series, and small cohort studies — most use in cardiac surgery vasoplegia, with additional reports in septic shock, liver transplant, and drug-induced (e.g. calcium channel blocker) vasoplegia. A 2023 systematic review noted a greater 1-hour MAP effect vs methylene blue but no mortality difference. NOT a TCCC recommendation; NOT an established trauma indication.
chunks.u: Refractory vasoplegic / distributive shock — NO scavenging rescue (investigational)

k: vitamin b12 analogue / cyanide antidote / nitric oxide scavenger
chunks.x:
Hydroxocobalamin (Cyanokit) for Hemorrhagic-shock-associated vasoplegia — mechanistic rationale only
Mechanistic extension: vasoplegia is described across advanced shock states including hemorrhagic shock, and NO scavenging is the proposed target. Direct clinical evidence in trauma/hemorrhagic shock is essentially absent — this is mechanistic rationale, not a validated indication. Listed for reasoning completeness; do not act on this in isolation.

DRUG: Ceftriaxone (Rocephin)
Class: 3rd generation cephalosporin / Beta-lactam
Category: abx
Levels: r12, pfc, ccatt
Primary use: Combat-wound antibiotic (parenteral); pneumonia; meningitis; sepsis; penetrating eye trauma
Mechanism: Binds penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs) → inhibits cell wall synthesis → bactericidal; broad gram-negative coverage; moderate gram-positive; penetrates CSF; once-daily IM or IV; biliary excretion (safe in renal failure)
WARNINGS: Biliary sludge with prolonged use. Do NOT mix with calcium-containing IV solutions (precipitation) — reconstitute in normal saline only, never Lactated Ringer's. Cross-reactivity with penicillin allergy (~1-2% true cross-reactivity).
Notes: Guidance on the parenteral combat-wound antibiotic has varied across TCCC updates (ceftriaxone vs ertapenem) — verify current unit SOP and medical direction. Broader availability and logistical practicality favor ceftriaxone in austere environments. Biliary excretion means no dose adjustment in renal failure.

Ceftriaxone (Rocephin) — R12 context: TCCC 2026 parenteral wound antibiotic of choice when the casualty cannot take oral medications (shock, unconsciousness): 2g IV/IO/IM once daily. Also the parenteral option for penetrating eye trauma. Replaced ertapenem (TCCC Change 25-1).

Ceftriaxone (Rocephin) — PFC context: TCCC 2026: 2g IV/IO/IM once daily for open combat wounds and invasive procedures when PO route unavailable. Penetrating eye trauma: 2g IV or IM. Also covers community-acquired pneumonia, meningitis, sepsis in prolonged field care.

Ceftriaxone (Rocephin) — CCATT context: IV 2g daily for wound prophylaxis. Meningitis 2g q12h. Sepsis empiric coverage. Combine with metronidazole for intraabdominal infections. Safe in renal failure — biliary excretion.

k: battlefield open wound / invasive procedure — tccc 2026 parenteral antibiotic of choice
chunks.x:
Ceftriaxone (Rocephin) for Battlefield open wound / invasive procedure — TCCC 2026 parenteral antibiotic of choice
TCCC 2026: for all open combat wounds and invasive procedures when the casualty is unable to take PO meds (shock, unconsciousness), give ceftriaxone 2g IV/IO/IM once daily. This replaced ertapenem under TCCC Change 25-1.
chunks.u: Battlefield open wound / invasive procedure — TCCC 2026 parenteral antibiotic of choice

chunks.x:
Ceftriaxone (Rocephin) for Penetrating eye trauma — TCCC 2026 indication
TCCC 2026: for penetrating eye injury, administer ceftriaxone 2g IV or IM as soon as possible (cefadroxil 1g PO is the oral alternative). Cover the eye with a rigid shield, not a pressure patch.

Ceftriaxone (Rocephin) for Bacterial meningitis — high-dose CSF penetration
2g IV q12h achieves therapeutic CSF concentrations; covers N. meningitidis, S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae. Combine with dexamethasone.

Ceftriaxone (Rocephin) for Sepsis empiric coverage — gram-negative bacteremia
Excellent gram-negative bactericidal coverage; first-line for gram-negative sepsis in deployed settings.

Ceftriaxone (Rocephin) for Lyme disease — IV treatment
2g IV daily for disseminated Lyme disease with neurological or cardiac involvement; deployed personnel in endemic areas.

Ceftriaxone (Rocephin) for Gonorrhea — single IM dose
500 mg IM single dose; relevant for deployed personnel in endemic areas.

Ceftriaxone (Rocephin) for Renal failure antibiotic — biliary excretion
Primarily excreted in bile → no dose adjustment in renal failure; preferred beta-lactam when renal function compromised.

DRUG: Azithromycin (Zithromax)
Class: Macrolide antibiotic / Anti-inflammatory
Category: abx
Levels: r12, pfc, ccatt
Primary use: Atypical pneumonia; STIs; Campylobacter diarrhea; anti-inflammatory
Mechanism: Binds 50S ribosomal subunit → inhibits protein synthesis → bacteriostatic (bactericidal at high concentrations); intracellular accumulation → effective against intracellular organisms; anti-inflammatory via NF-κB inhibition and macrophage modulation independent of antimicrobial effect; long tissue half-life (3-5 days)
WARNINGS: QT prolongation — avoid with other QT-prolonging agents. Hepatotoxicity rare. Resistance increasing globally for many organisms. Drug interactions via CYP3A4.
Notes: Anti-inflammatory mechanism is separate from antimicrobial — explains benefit in non-infectious inflammatory airway conditions. Long tissue half-life means 5-day tissue levels after 3-day course.

Azithromycin (Zithromax) — R12 context: Mission-degrading diarrhea treatment: azithromycin 500 mg daily x3 days for Campylobacter (ciprofloxacin-resistant). Respiratory tract infections. STI treatment (1g single dose for chlamydia).
Azithromycin (Zithromax) — PFC context: Atypical pneumonia coverage to combine with ceftriaxone. Anti-inflammatory bronchitis management. Traveler's diarrhea when ciprofloxacin resistance suspected.
Azithromycin (Zithromax) — CCATT context: Pneumonia combination therapy. Anti-inflammatory adjunct in ARDS and diffuse alveolar damage. Prophylaxis in immunocompromised.

Azithromycin (Zithromax) for Campylobacter diarrhea — ciprofloxacin resistance
Ciprofloxacin resistance in Campylobacter >50% in many regions. Azithromycin 500 mg daily x3 days is now preferred for Campylobacter traveler's diarrhea.

Azithromycin (Zithromax) for Anti-inflammatory in ARDS / diffuse bronchiolitis
NF-κB inhibition + macrophage modulation independent of antimicrobial effect; studied for ARDS adjunct and post-viral bronchiolitis.

Azithromycin (Zithromax) for Chlamydia/STI treatment — single dose
1g PO single dose for chlamydia; relevant for PFC deployed personnel.

Azithromycin (Zithromax) for MAC prophylaxis in immunocompromised
Weekly azithromycin 1200 mg for MAC prophylaxis in HIV/immunosuppressed patients.

DRUG: Flumazenil (Romazicon)
Class: Competitive benzodiazepine receptor antagonist
Category: antidote
Levels: pfc, ccatt
Primary use: Benzodiazepine overdose reversal; procedural sedation reversal
Mechanism: Competitive antagonism at GABA-A benzodiazepine binding site → reverses benzodiazepine-induced CNS/respiratory depression; short duration (30-60 min) — SHORTER than most benzodiazepines → re-sedation expected; does NOT reverse other sedatives (opioids, barbiturates, propofol)
WARNINGS: Duration (30-60 min) SHORTER than most benzodiazepines — RE-SEDATION EXPECTED. Multiple doses or infusion may be required. Will precipitate acute withdrawal in BZD-dependent patients. Does NOT reverse opioids, barbiturates, or propofol.
Notes: Mirror image of naloxone: diagnostic + reversal for its drug class. Same re-sedation vigilance required. Does NOT work for non-BZD sedatives.

Flumazenil (Romazicon) — PFC context: Benzodiazepine OD reversal in PFC. Diagnostic challenge for undifferentiated sedation. 0.2 mg IV q1 min to effect (max 1 mg). Duration shorter than most benzos — monitor for re-sedation.
Flumazenil (Romazicon) — CCATT context: Procedural sedation reversal. BZD OD during CASEVAC. Diagnostic for comatose patients. Re-sedation monitoring protocol essential during transport.

Flumazenil (Romazicon) for Diagnostic challenge — undifferentiated sedation/coma
If AMS reverses with flumazenil → benzodiazepine etiology confirmed. Guides management without imaging in resource-limited settings. Same diagnostic principle as naloxone for opioids.

Flumazenil (Romazicon) for Procedural sedation reversal
Reverse midazolam after procedures when prolonged sedation undesired; enables faster recovery and extubation.

Flumazenil (Romazicon) for Hepatic encephalopathy (research)
Endogenous BZD-like substances accumulate in hepatic failure; flumazenil may transiently improve HE — investigational.

k: endogenous purine nucleoside / av nodal blocker
endogenous nucleoside / av nodal blocker / svt terminator
chunks.x:
DRUG: Adenosine (Adenocard)
Class: Endogenous purine nucleoside / AV nodal blocker / SVT terminator
Category: cardiac
Levels: pfc, ccatt
Primary use: SVT (supraventricular tachycardia) termination; diagnostic for wide-complex tachycardia. SVT (PSVT) conversion; stable narrow-complex tachycardia diagnosis; WPW-associated SVT (avoid)
Mechanism: Activates A1 adenosine receptors → hyperpolarizes AV nodal cells → transient AV block (6-12 seconds) → interrupts re-entrant SVT circuits; endogenous molecule with ultra-short half-life (<10 seconds) → effects fully reversible in seconds; diagnostic: adenosine-sensitive SVT terminates, VT does not. Activates A1 adenosine receptors in AV node → hyperpolarization → transient AV block → interrupts reentrant circuits → terminates SVT; half-life 10 seconds → effect lasts only 20-30 seconds; must be given as rapid IV push followed immediately by saline flush; diagnostic: transiently slows ventricular rate to reveal atrial flutter waves
WARNINGS: Must give as RAPID IV push followed immediately by saline flush — half-life <10 seconds means slow push = ineffective. Causes transient chest tightness, flushing, dyspnea — warn patient. CONTRAINDICATED in 2nd/3rd degree AV block, sick sinus syndrome, WPW with wide complex. MUST give as rapid IV push (1-2 sec) + immediate 20 mL flush — slow infusion is ineffective (10-sec half-life). CONTRAINDICATED in WPW with atrial fibrillation (irregular wide-complex) — may accelerate conduction via accessory pathway → VF. Asthma: causes bronchospasm — use verapamil instead. Patients on dipyridamole: reduce dose to 3 mg.
Notes: Rapid push technique is everything: adenosine 6 mg rapid push → immediate 20 mL NS flush → raise arm. Peripheral antecubital vein acceptable if central unavailable. Adenosine technique is everything: rapid push into large antecubital or central line immediately followed by 20 mL saline bolus. Patients should be warned of transient flushing, chest tightness, and sense of doom (brief, 20-30 sec). Have crash cart ready.

k: endogenous purine nucleoside / av nodal blocker
chunks.x: Adenosine (Adenocard) — PFC context: SVT in PFC — 6 mg rapid IV push followed immediately by 20 mL saline flush. MUST use antecubital or central vein (rapid central delivery). If no effect in 1-2 min, 12 mg repeat.

k: endogenous purine nucleoside / av nodal blocker
chunks.x: Adenosine (Adenocard) — CCATT context: Full SVT management protocol. Diagnostic for wide-complex tachycardia. Theophylline-related tachycardia may require higher doses. Have atropine ready for prolonged block.

k: endogenous purine nucleoside / av nodal blocker
chunks.x:
Adenosine (Adenocard) for Diagnostic — SVT vs VT differentiation
Adenosine terminates AV-nodal-dependent SVT but NOT VT. Temporary AV block during VT reveals the underlying rhythm. Critical diagnostic tool when ECG interpretation uncertain.

k: endogenous purine nucleoside / av nodal blocker
chunks.x:
Adenosine (Adenocard) for Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) — narrow complex SVT only
Terminates AV-nodal-dependent tachycardia in WPW when accessory pathway not conducting antegradely. CONTRAINDICATED in pre-excited AF/WPW with wide complex.

k: endogenous purine nucleoside / av nodal blocker
stress testing — pharmacological nuclear stress test
chunks.x:
Adenosine (Adenocard) for Stress testing — pharmacological nuclear stress test
Adenosine coronary vasodilation used for nuclear stress testing in patients unable to exercise; identifies coronary artery disease.
chunks.u: Stress testing — pharmacological nuclear stress test

chunks.x:
DRUG: Dopamine
Class: Endogenous catecholamine / Dose-dependent receptor agonist
Category: vasoactive
Levels: pfc, ccatt
Primary use: Hemodynamically significant bradycardia; cardiogenic shock; vasopressor support
Mechanism: Dose-dependent receptor activation: low (2-5 mcg/kg/min) → dopaminergic (DA1/DA2) → renal/mesenteric vasodilation; moderate (5-10) → β1 → inotropy/chronotropy; high (>10) → α1 → vasoconstriction; endogenous catecholamine precursor to norepinephrine
WARNINGS: Higher arrhythmia risk than norepinephrine — particularly atrial fibrillation. Extravasation causes tissue necrosis. Renal-dose dopamine (2-3 mcg/kg/min) does NOT protect kidneys — largely abandoned.
Notes: The "renal dose" concept (2-3 mcg/kg/min to protect kidneys) has been disproven — do not use for renal protection. Use for hemodynamic indications only.
Dopamine — PFC context: Bradycardia unresponsive to atropine when external pacing unavailable. Cardiogenic shock in PFC. 5-20 mcg/kg/min titrated.

Dopamine — CCATT context: Second-line vasopressor when norepinephrine unavailable. Septic shock in pediatric patients (relatively more evidence). Bradycardia support. Renal-dose dopamine (controversial — largely abandoned).

Dopamine for Bradycardia — chronotropic when atropine fails
Beta-1 agonism increases heart rate; used for symptomatic bradycardia when atropine ineffective and external pacing unavailable.

Dopamine for Cardiogenic shock — inotropy + vasoconstriction
Combined β1 (inotropy) + α1 (vasoconstriction) at moderate-high doses; alternative to dobutamine + norepinephrine combination when single agent preferred.

Dopamine for Pediatric septic shock — relatively preferred
More pediatric evidence than norepinephrine for septic shock; dopaminergic receptors more prominent in pediatric physiology.

DRUG: Lorazepam (Ativan)
Class: Benzodiazepine / GABA-A modulator / Long-acting anticonvulsant
Category: analgesia
Levels: pfc, ccatt
Primary use: Status epilepticus; severe anxiety; alcohol withdrawal; ICU sedation
Mechanism: Positive allosteric GABA-A receptor modulator → enhances Cl⁻ influx → CNS depression, anticonvulsant, anxiolysis, muscle relaxation; longer duration than midazolam (4-8h); reliable IM absorption (unlike diazepam); less lipophilic than midazolam → slower CNS penetration but longer effect
WARNINGS: Respiratory depression — particularly with opioids. Propylene glycol vehicle in IV formulation → toxicity with high-dose prolonged infusion. Accumulates in obesity and hepatic failure.
Notes: IM lorazepam is as effective as IV for status epilepticus when given promptly (RAMPART trial). Tactical advantage: reliable IM absorption unlike diazepam.
Lorazepam (Ativan) — PFC context: Status epilepticus when midazolam unavailable. IM lorazepam 4 mg for seizure. Alcohol withdrawal management in PFC. Severe anxiety/agitation.

Lorazepam (Ativan) — CCATT context: ICU sedation protocol. Status epilepticus second-line. Alcohol/benzo withdrawal titration. CIWA protocol. Longer acting than midazolam — useful for sustained sedation.

k: status epilepticus — im when iv unavailable
chunks.x:
Lorazepam (Ativan) for Status epilepticus — IM when IV unavailable
4 mg IM lorazepam; reliable IM absorption unlike diazepam. Evidence: equivalent to IV lorazepam in RAMPART trial when IM given promptly.
chunks.u: Status epilepticus — IM when IV unavailable

chunks.x:
Lorazepam (Ativan) for Alcohol withdrawal — CIWA-based protocol
Symptom-triggered lorazepam dosing per CIWA score; prevents withdrawal seizures and delirium tremens. Longer half-life than midazolam = smoother titration.

k: icu sedation — longer duration than midazolam
chunks.x:
Lorazepam (Ativan) for ICU sedation — longer duration than midazolam
4-6 mg IV q2-4h or infusion; provides sustained sedation; less accumulation than diazepam.
chunks.u: ICU sedation — longer duration than midazolam

chunks.x:
Lorazepam (Ativan) for Acute panic/anxiety — combat stress reaction
0.5-2 mg IM/PO for acute panic or combat stress reaction with severe anxiety; short-term use only.

DRUG: Phenobarbital
Class: Barbiturate / GABA-A modulator / Anticonvulsant
Category: analgesia
Levels: ccatt
Primary use: Refractory status epilepticus; neonatal seizures; alcohol withdrawal refractory to BZD
Mechanism: Direct GABA-A receptor agonist (unlike BZDs which are allosteric modulators) → opens Cl⁻ channel directly → more potent CNS depression; also inhibits glutamate AMPA receptors; burst suppression at high doses; very long half-life (80-120h) → loading dose approach
WARNINGS: Respiratory depression — intubation often required with loading dose. Hypotension during IV loading. Very long half-life means effects persist days. Drug interactions via CYP450 induction.
Notes: Key difference from BZDs: direct GABA-A agonist vs allosteric modulator — explains efficacy when BZDs fail (downregulated receptors). Neonatal seizures: phenobarbital is first-line (not BZDs).

Phenobarbital — CCATT context: Third-line status epilepticus after BZD + phenytoin/levetiracetam failure. 20 mg/kg IV load at 50-100 mg/min. Refractory alcohol withdrawal when BZDs insufficient. Neonatal seizures.

Phenobarbital for Refractory status epilepticus — third line
20 mg/kg IV load after BZD + phenytoin failure. Direct GABA-A agonism works when allosteric modulation (BZDs) is insufficient.

Phenobarbital for Refractory alcohol withdrawal — BZD-resistant
Some alcohol withdrawal patients are BZD-resistant due to GABA receptor downregulation; phenobarbital as direct agonist bypasses this resistance.

Phenobarbital for Neonatal seizures — first-line
20 mg/kg IV; first-line for neonatal seizures (unlike adults where BZDs are first-line); different receptor pharmacology in neonates.

k: icp — burst suppression for refractory intracranial hypertension
chunks.x:
Phenobarbital for ICP — burst suppression for refractory intracranial hypertension
High-dose phenobarbital burst suppression reduces CMRO2 and ICP when other measures fail; alternative to pentobarbital coma.
chunks.u: ICP — burst suppression for refractory intracranial hypertension

chunks.x:
DRUG: Methoxyflurane (Penthrox)
Class: Inhaled analgesic / Volatile halogenated ether
Category: analgesia
Levels: pfc
Primary use: Self-administered inhaled analgesia; acute pain; trauma pain
Mechanism: Inhaled low-dose methoxyflurane → CNS depression of pain pathways via NMDA antagonism, voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channel inhibition, and GABA-A modulation → rapid-onset (6-10 sec) analgesia without loss of consciousness; metabolized partially in liver → fluoride ion (nephrotoxicity at anesthetic doses, NOT analgesic doses)
WARNINGS: Limited to 6 mL per treatment episode. NOT for anesthetic doses (nephrotoxicity and hepatotoxicity at higher doses). Avoid in renal failure. Avoid in history of malignant hyperthermia.
Notes: Not yet FDA-approved in US but used by Australian and UK military SOF. Self-limiting mechanism (patient drops inhaler if over-sedated) makes it uniquely safe for self-administration.

Methoxyflurane (Penthrox) — SOF context: Australian/UK SOF standard. Self-administered via Green Whistle inhaler — patient controls their own analgesia. Rapid onset, no IV needed, no overdose risk (patient drops inhaler if over-sedated). Ideal for combat casualty self-care.

Methoxyflurane (Penthrox) for Self-administered analgesia — no medic needed
Patient inhales as needed; self-limiting (drops inhaler if over-sedated). No IV, no needle, no monitoring needed. Transforms casualty self-care capability.

k: procedural analgesia — wound care, dressing changes
chunks.x:
Methoxyflurane (Penthrox) for Procedural analgesia — wound care, dressing changes
Short-duration inhaled analgesia for painful procedures; 3 mL provides 25-30 min of analgesia.
chunks.u: Procedural analgesia — wound care, dressing changes

Methoxyflurane (Penthrox) for Pediatric/civilian trauma — non-invasive

DRUG: Whole Blood / Blood Products (pRBC, FFP, PLT)
Class: Blood component / Oxygen carrier / Coagulation factor source
Category: hemostasis
Levels: pfc, ccatt
Primary use: Hemorrhagic shock resuscitation; massive transfusion; coagulopathy correction
Mechanism: pRBC: restores O2-carrying capacity via hemoglobin; FFP: replaces all coagulation factors (I, II, V, VII, VIII, IX, X, XI); PLT: restores platelet-mediated primary hemostasis; Whole Blood: all three simultaneously — most physiologically complete resuscitation fluid; low-titer group O whole blood (LTOWB) is current JTS standard
WARNINGS: Type and cross-match when possible. LTOWB is type O — use judiciously in female casualties of childbearing age (Rh sensitization). Warm ALL blood products. Calcium replacement MANDATORY with every 4 units.
Notes: JTS current standard: LTOWB > 1:1:1 components > crystalloid. Never give crystalloid as primary resuscitation fluid in hemorrhagic shock. Each unit of whole blood = ~18 mmol citrate → calcium replacement critical.

DRUG: Supplemental Oxygen
Class: Medical gas / Oxygen therapy
Category: airway
Levels: r12, pfc, ccatt
Primary use: Hypoxia; respiratory distress; CO poisoning; TBI; chest injuries
Mechanism: Increases FiO2 → increases dissolved O2 in plasma and hemoglobin O2 saturation → improves tissue oxygen delivery; in CO poisoning: high FiO2 competes with CO for hemoglobin binding → accelerates COHb clearance (half-life: room air 5h → 100% O2 60-90 min)
WARNINGS: HYPEROXIA is harmful in post-cardiac arrest (ROSC) and COPD — titrate to SpO2 94-98%, not 100%. O2 supports combustion — no open flames. Limited supply in field — conserve.
Notes: CO poisoning: 100% O2 NRB is mandatory and urgent. SpO2 pulse oximetry is FALSELY NORMAL in CO poisoning — CO-oximetry required for accurate COHb measurement.

Supplemental Oxygen — R12 context: Pulse ox <94% → apply O2. Penetrating chest trauma, tension pneumothorax post-decompression, hemorrhagic shock. NRB mask or nasal cannula. Monitor SpO2. Limited O2 supply — use judiciously.
Supplemental Oxygen — PFC context: Full O2 management. Hyperbaric-equivalent CO treatment with NRB at 15L/min. Post-airway management O2. Smoke inhalation high-flow O2.
Supplemental Oxygen — CCATT context: Ventilator O2 management. 100% O2 for CO poisoning. Titrate FiO2 to SpO2 94-98% (avoid hyperoxia in post-cardiac arrest and COPD).

Supplemental Oxygen for CO poisoning — accelerates COHb clearance
100% O2 via NRB reduces CO half-life from 5 hours (room air) to 60-90 minutes. High-flow O2 is first-line for all CO/smoke inhalation casualties.

Supplemental Oxygen for Cluster headache — abortive treatment
100% O2 at 10-15 L/min via NRB for 15-20 min aborts cluster headache attacks in 70-80% of cases.

Supplemental Oxygen for TBI — prevent secondary hypoxic injury
Maintain SpO2 >94% in TBI. Hypoxia is a major secondary injury driver. Hyperoxia also harmful in post-cardiac arrest — titrate carefully.

Supplemental Oxygen for Pneumothorax post-decompression — nitrogen washout
High-flow O2 washes out nitrogen from pneumothorax cavity → accelerates spontaneous reabsorption of small PTX.

DRUG: Ipratropium (Atrovent)
Class: Short-acting muscarinic antagonist (SAMA) / Anticholinergic bronchodilator
Category: airway
Levels: pfc, ccatt
Primary use: COPD exacerbation; bronchospasm adjunct; secretion reduction
Mechanism: Blocks muscarinic M3 receptors on airway smooth muscle → prevents acetylcholine-mediated bronchoconstriction → bronchodilation; also reduces airway secretions; does NOT cross BBB (quaternary ammonium) → no systemic anticholinergic effects; additive with beta-agonists via different mechanism
WARNINGS: Paradoxical bronchospasm rare but possible. Avoid in narrow-angle glaucoma (nebulized form can reach eyes). Urinary retention in BPH.
Notes: Combination albuterol + ipratropium (Combivent/DuoNeb) is standard for COPD exacerbations. Different mechanism = additive effect without increased side effects.
Ipratropium (Atrovent) — PFC context: Add to albuterol for refractory bronchospasm — different mechanism, additive effect. COPD exacerbation management. Secretion reduction pre-intubation.
Ipratropium (Atrovent) — CCATT context: Nebulized with albuterol for COPD/asthma. Ventilator patient bronchodilation. Secretion management in intubated patients.

Ipratropium (Atrovent) for Refractory bronchospasm — additive with albuterol
Ipratropium + albuterol = dual bronchodilation via different mechanisms (anticholinergic + beta-agonist). Combination reduces hospitalization vs either alone in COPD exacerbations.

chunks.x:
DRUG: Dextrose (D50W / D10W)
Class: Hypertonic glucose solution / Hypoglycemia antidote / HDIE vehicle
Category: electrolyte
Levels: r12, pfc, ccatt
Primary use: Severe hypoglycemia; insulin-glucose hyperkalemia protocol; HDIE vehicle
Mechanism: Exogenous glucose → immediate CNS substrate restoration → reverses neuroglycopenia; insulin co-administration activates Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase → K⁺ intracellular shift; D50W (2500 mOsm/L) = hyperosmolar → peripheral extravasation risk → tissue necrosis; D10W (500 mOsm/L) = safer peripherally, equivalent efficacy, lower rebound hyperglycemia
WARNINGS: D50W peripheral extravasation → severe tissue necrosis. Prefer D10W peripherally. ALWAYS give thiamine before dextrose in alcoholics/malnourished. Monitor glucose q30 min during insulin infusion.
Notes: D10W vs D50W: equivalent efficacy for hypoglycemia (Moore & Woollard 2005 RCT — median 8 min to GCS 15 both groups), but D10W gives less rebound hyperglycemia and safer peripherally. D50W still preferred when speed is critical.

DRUG: Diphenhydramine (Benadryl)
Class: First-generation H1 antihistamine / Anticholinergic / Sedative
Category: analgesia
Levels: r12, pfc, ccatt
Primary use: Anaphylaxis adjunct; allergic reactions; urticaria; motion sickness
Mechanism: Competitive H1 receptor antagonism → blocks histamine-mediated vasodilation, bronchospasm, urticaria, pruritus; crosses BBB (first-generation) → sedation, antiemetic, antivertigo; anticholinergic effects → drying of secretions, smooth muscle relaxation; does NOT reverse life-threatening anaphylaxis — epinephrine does
WARNINGS: CRITICAL: Diphenhydramine does NOT treat anaphylaxis — epinephrine FIRST always. Sedation impairs casualty assessment. Anticholinergic effects may mask tachycardia. Avoid in TBI (CNS depression).
Notes: Anaphylaxis teaching point: H1 blocker + H2 blocker (ranitidine/famotidine) + dexamethasone + epinephrine = complete anaphylaxis protocol. Diphenhydramine is the H1 component only.

Diphenhydramine (Benadryl) — R12 context: Anaphylaxis ADJUNCT after epinephrine — 25-50 mg IV/IM. Allergic reactions to food, medications, insect stings. Do NOT substitute for epinephrine. Urticaria and pruritus management.

Diphenhydramine (Benadryl) — PFC context: Full allergic reaction management. Anaphylaxis protocol: epi FIRST, then diphenhydramine + ranitidine + dexamethasone. Dystonic reaction reversal from haloperidol/prochlorperazine.
Diphenhydramine (Benadryl) — CCATT context: IV 25-50 mg for allergic reactions. Dystonic reaction reversal. Motion sickness during CASEVAC. Sleep aid in prolonged care.

Diphenhydramine (Benadryl) for Extrapyramidal / dystonic reaction reversal
25-50 mg IV/IM rapidly reverses acute dystonic reactions from antipsychotics (haloperidol, prochlorperazine) or metoclopramide via anticholinergic mechanism. Mission-critical when using antipsychotics for behavioral emergencies.

Diphenhydramine (Benadryl) for Anaphylaxis adjunct — H1 blockade
After epinephrine controls life-threatening symptoms, diphenhydramine 50 mg IV reduces ongoing histamine-mediated urticaria and angioedema. Part of multi-drug anaphylaxis protocol.

Diphenhydramine (Benadryl) for Motion sickness — vestibular H1 blockade
H1 and muscarinic antagonism reduces vestibular input to vomiting center; effective for CASEVAC helicopter/aircraft motion sickness prevention.

Diphenhydramine (Benadryl) for Sedation adjunct — acute agitation
25-50 mg IV/IM provides mild sedation for agitated patients when dedicated sedatives limited; additive with low-dose haloperidol.

chunks.x:
DRUG: Haloperidol (Haldol)
Class: Typical antipsychotic / D2 receptor antagonist / Butyrophenone / First-generation antipsychotic / D2 dopamine antagonist
Category: analgesia
Levels: pfc, ccatt
Primary use: Acute agitation; behavioral emergency; delirium; ICU sedation adjunct. ICU delirium and agitation; acute psychosis; B52 chemical restraint; nausea (antiemetic); Tourette syndrome
Mechanism: Potent D2 dopamine receptor antagonism → antipsychotic + sedation; some H1 and α1 blockade; less respiratory depression than benzodiazepines; IV form for acute agitation; long half-life (24h) → sustained effect; lower seizure threshold; EPS risk via nigrostriatal D2 blockade. Potent D2 dopamine receptor blockade → antipsychotic and antiemetic effects; also blocks D1, alpha-1, H1, and muscarinic receptors; IV/IM formulations available; less sedating than BZDs; DOES NOT reduce delirium duration (AID-ICU, MIND-USA trials) but reduces agitation severity and benzodiazepine requirements; QTc prolongation but clinically safe up to QTc 550 ms (MIND-USA secondary analysis)
WARNINGS: QT prolongation — monitor ECG with IV use. EPS (extrapyramidal symptoms) and acute dystonia — have diphenhydramine ready. Do NOT combine olanzapine IM + lorazepam IM (fatal respiratory depression reported). NMS risk. QTc prolongation (monitor, but MIND-USA: safe up to QTc 550 ms). Extrapyramidal reactions (dystonia, akathisia) — treat with diphenhydramine 25-50 mg IV. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (rare but life-threatening: hyperthermia + rigidity + autonomic instability). Do NOT combine IM haloperidol with IV promethazine (extravasation risk).
Notes: B52 protocol: haloperidol 5 mg + midazolam 5 mg + promethazine 50 mg IM = rapid behavioral control in austere setting. Diphenhydramine 50 mg IV immediately reverses acute dystonic reaction. ICU delirium evidence update: haloperidol does NOT reduce delirium-free days (AID-ICU 2022, MIND-USA 2018) — but does reduce agitation, benzodiazepine use, and intrusive memories (EuRIDICE 2023). Use for agitation control, not as delirium cure.

chunks.x:
DRUG: Levetiracetam (Keppra)
Class: Novel antiepileptic / SV2A synaptic vesicle protein modulator
Category: analgesia
Levels: pfc, ccatt
Primary use: Status epilepticus (second-line); seizure prophylaxis in TBI; maintenance anticonvulsant
Mechanism: Binds SV2A (synaptic vesicle protein 2A) → modulates neurotransmitter release; does NOT act on GABA or glutamate directly; unique mechanism explains activity when GABA-modulating drugs (BZDs, phenobarbital) fail; minimal drug interactions (no CYP450); renal clearance; no hepatotoxicity; no enzyme induction

DRUG: Mannitol 20%
Class: Osmotic diuretic / ICP-reducing agent / Renal protective agent
Category: electrolyte
Levels: pfc, ccatt
Primary use: Raised intracranial pressure; cerebral edema; acute glaucoma; rhabdomyolysis diuresis
Mechanism: Osmotic agent → increases serum osmolality → draws free water from cerebral edema into vasculature → reduces ICP; induces osmotic diuresis (renal) → reduces edema and flushes myoglobin; does NOT cross BBB normally; onset 15-30 min; duration 3-8h; 0.5-1 g/kg IV over 15-20 min for ICP crisis
WARNINGS: Monitor serum osmolality q4-6h — STOP if >320 mOsm (rebound cerebral edema). MUST maintain euvolemia — hypotension worsens TBI. Contraindicated in anuria/severe renal failure. Crystallization at low temperatures — warm before use.
Notes: Mannitol vs hypertonic saline for ICP: both effective; hypertonic saline preferred when patient is hypovolemic (no diuretic effect); mannitol preferred with adequate volume status. JTS CPG: mannitol 1g/kg for herniation.

chunks.x:
DRUG: Hypertonic Saline 3% / 23.4%
Class: Osmotic agent / ICP-reducing agent / Hyponatremia correction / Resuscitation fluid
Category: electrolyte
Levels: r12, pfc, ccatt
Primary use: Raised ICP; severe hyponatremia with symptoms; traumatic brain injury; small-volume resuscitation
Mechanism: Hypertonic NaCl → increases serum osmolality → draws free water from cerebral edema into intravascular space → reduces ICP; also increases intravascular volume (small-volume resuscitation — 250 mL 3% = 1L isotonic effect); corrects hyponatremia; immunomodulatory effects
WARNINGS: 23.4% NaCl — CENTRAL LINE REQUIRED (extreme osmolarity 8000 mOsm). Peripheral 3% NaCl acceptable. Hyponatremia correction — MAXIMUM 8-10 mEq/L per 24h; faster correction → osmotic demyelination syndrome (permanent neurological damage). TCCC 2026: do not use hypertonic saline prophylactically to prevent herniation; hypertonic saline is NOT a resuscitative fluid.
Notes: Osmotic demyelination (central pontine myelinolysis) from over-rapid hyponatremia correction is IRREVERSIBLE. If Na⁺ correction >10 mEq/L in 24h detected — immediately STOP HTS and give free water or DDAVP to lower Na⁺.

Class: Glycopeptide antibiotic / Cell wall synthesis inhibitor
Category: abx

DRUG: Metronidazole (Flagyl)
Class: Nitroimidazole antibiotic + antiprotozoal / DNA disruptor
Category: abx
Levels: r12, pfc, ccatt
Primary use: Anaerobic infections; intraabdominal sepsis; C. diff; trichomoniasis; giardia; amebic dysentery
Mechanism: Reduced by anaerobic organisms to toxic nitro radical → damages bacterial DNA → bactericidal; selective for anaerobes and certain protozoa (Trichomonas, Giardia, Entamoeba); excellent tissue penetration including abscess cavities and CNS; disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol

Notes: Metronidazole is irreplaceable for protozoal GI infections (Giardia, amebiasis) in deployed settings where these are common. No other standard formulary drug covers this gap.

Metronidazole (Flagyl) — R12 context: Combat diarrhea from Giardia/ameba in austere environments. Penetrating abdominal trauma anaerobic coverage (with ciprofloxacin). Simple outpatient treatment for most protozoal GI infections.

Metronidazole (Flagyl) — PFC context: Intraabdominal infections with ciprofloxacin. Anaerobic wound infections (necrotizing fasciitis component). Traveler's diarrhea from Giardia or ameba. PO for less severe infections.

Metronidazole (Flagyl) — CCATT context: IV for severe intraabdominal sepsis. C. diff first-line alternative (mild cases). Abdominal abscess. Combination with ceftriaxone or ciprofloxacin for full polymicrobial coverage.

k: natural glucocorticoid + mineralocorticoid / stress dose steroid

DRUG: Hydrocortisone (Solu-Cortef)
Class: Natural glucocorticoid + mineralocorticoid / Stress dose steroid
Category: antiinflam
Levels: pfc, ccatt
Primary use: Adrenal insufficiency; septic shock adjunct; anaphylaxis adjunct; stress dose coverage
Mechanism: Natural cortisol; both glucocorticoid (anti-inflammatory, metabolic) AND mineralocorticoid (Na⁺ retention, K⁺ excretion) activity; stress dose (200 mg/day) replaces deficient cortisol in critical illness; vasopressor-sensitizing effect in septic shock; unlike dexamethasone — provides mineralocorticoid replacement

Class: Selective α2 adrenergic agonist / Sedative-analgesic / Non-GABA sedative
Category: analgesia
Levels: ccatt
Primary use: ICU sedation; cooperative/light sedation; opioid-sparing; ventilator weaning; alcohol withdrawal adjunct

DRUG: Phenylephrine (Neo-Synephrine)
Class: Pure α1 adrenergic agonist / Vasopressor
Category: vasoactive
Levels: pfc, ccatt
Primary use: Vasodilatory hypotension without cardiac compromise; spinal/neuraxial anesthesia hypotension; SVT (vagal)
Mechanism: Pure α1 receptor agonism → vasoconstriction → increased SVR and MAP; NO β1 effect → no increase in heart rate (may cause reflex bradycardia); no β2 effect; predictable dose-response; short duration (15-20 min IV bolus); useful when tachycardia is already present and norepinephrine not available
WARNINGS: Reflex bradycardia — monitor HR. Avoid in cardiogenic shock (pure vasoconstriction increases afterload without inotropy). Tissue necrosis with extravasation. Renal/mesenteric vasoconstriction with high doses.
Notes: Key tactical use: anesthesia hypotension during field surgery — phenylephrine 100-200 mcg IV bolus rapidly corrects spinal hypotension without cardiac effects. Phentolamine for extravasation.

Pure α1 vasoconstriction restores MAP without cardiac stimulation; preferred vasopressor for spinal anesthesia in obstetric emergencies (fetal acidosis less than with ephedrine).

Phenylephrine (Neo-Synephrine) for SVT — reflex bradycardia induction (Bezold-Jarisch reflex)

k: fat-soluble vitamin / coagulation factor synthesis cofactor / warfarin antidote
chunks.x:
DRUG: Vitamin K (Phytonadione) / PCC
Class: Fat-soluble vitamin / Coagulation factor synthesis cofactor / Warfarin antidote
Category: hemostasis
Levels: pfc, ccatt
Primary use: Warfarin reversal; anticoagulant overdose; coagulation factor deficiency; bleeding in anticoagulated casualty
Mechanism: Vitamin K: cofactor for carboxylation of factors II, VII, IX, X (and proteins C, S) → restores synthesis of vitamin K-dependent coagulation factors; slow onset (6-24h for effect). PCC (Prothrombin Complex Concentrate): contains factors II, VII, IX, X directly → IMMEDIATE coagulation restoration (minutes); bypasses 6-24h wait for vitamin K synthesis
WARNINGS: PCC contains heparin — contraindicated in HIT. Thrombotic risk with PCC — use only for life-threatening hemorrhage. Vitamin K IV: anaphylactic reactions possible (rare) — give slowly over 20-30 min. Warfarin effect may return if PCC given without Vitamin K.
Notes: Teaching point: PCC gives IMMEDIATE reversal (minutes) but effect wanes; Vitamin K takes 6-24h but provides DURABLE reversal. Always give both together for warfarin-related life-threatening hemorrhage.

k: skeletal muscle relaxant / ryanodine receptor antagonist / mh antidote
chunks.x:
DRUG: Dantrolene (Dantrium)
Class: Skeletal muscle relaxant / Ryanodine receptor antagonist / MH antidote
Category: analgesia
Levels: ccatt
Primary use: Malignant hyperthermia (MH); neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS); exertional heat stroke; severe spasticity
Mechanism: Blocks ryanodine receptor (RyR1) on sarcoplasmic reticulum → prevents Ca²⁺ release → prevents muscle contraction → reduces hyperthermia from uncontrolled muscle activity; ONLY specific pharmacological treatment for MH; also reduces Ca²⁺-mediated heat generation in NMS and exertional hyperthermia
WARNINGS: MUST HAVE dantrolene available whenever succinylcholine is used — MH is rapidly fatal without it. Each 20 mg vial requires 60 mL sterile water to reconstitute — labor intensive. Hepatotoxicity with chronic use.
Notes: MH protocol: STOP triggering agent → dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg IV q5 min until resolved → active cooling → sodium bicarbonate for acidosis → hyperkalemia management → ICU transfer.

chunks.x:
DRUG: Etomidate (Amidate)
Class: Non-barbiturate hypnotic / GABA-A modulator / RSI induction agent
Category: analgesia
Levels: pfc, ccatt
Primary use: RSI induction — hemodynamically neutral; cardiovascular compromise; status epilepticus induction
Mechanism: GABA-A receptor positive modulation → rapid sedation (15-30 sec) without analgesia; NO cardiovascular depression (unlike propofol) → no hypotension, no myocardial depression; NO bronchodilation (unlike ketamine); minimal histamine release; SINGLE DOSE adrenal suppression (blocks 11β-hydroxylase) — clinical significance debated in non-septic trauma patients

Notes: Jabre et al. RCT and meta-analysis: no significant difference in post-intubation hypotension between ketamine and etomidate. In trauma (non-septic), adrenal suppression clinical significance is minimal.

chunks.x:
DRUG: Furosemide (Lasix)
Class: Loop diuretic / Na⁺-K⁺-2Cl⁻ cotransporter inhibitor
Category: electrolyte
Levels: pfc, ccatt
Primary use: Acute pulmonary edema; fluid overload; hypertensive emergency; hypercalcemia; hyperkalemia adjunct
Mechanism: Inhibits Na⁺-K⁺-2Cl⁻ cotransporter in thick ascending loop of Henle → inhibits renal NaCl reabsorption → profound natriuresis and diuresis; also direct venodilation (independent of diuresis) → rapid preload reduction in pulmonary edema within minutes of IV administration; onset IV: 5-10 min; peak: 20-60 min
WARNINGS: Hypokalemia — monitor K⁺; replace aggressively. Hypomagnesemia common. Ototoxicity with rapid high-dose IV (>4 mg/min). Contraindicated in sulfa allergy (cross-reactivity). Prerenal AKI with overdiuresis.
Notes: DOSE trial (NEJM 2011): bolus vs continuous infusion equivalent efficacy; high-dose (2.5× oral dose) more effective than low-dose without significant renal harm. For ADHF: high-dose bolus is preferred.

Furosemide (Lasix) — PFC context: Flash pulmonary edema in prolonged field care. Hypertensive emergency with pulmonary edema. 40-80 mg IV. Hypercalcemia (with IV fluids). Deployed medical support for casualties with CHF exacerbation.

Furosemide (Lasix) — CCATT context: Full diuresis protocol. Acute decompensated heart failure. 40-200 mg IV. Continuous infusion for refractory edema. Renal protection (osmotic diuresis). Electrolyte monitoring mandatory.

k: water-soluble b vitamin / cofactor for glucose metabolism / wernicke prophylaxis
chunks.x:
DRUG: Thiamine (Vitamin B1)
Class: Water-soluble B vitamin / Cofactor for glucose metabolism / Wernicke prophylaxis
Category: electrolyte
Levels: r12, pfc, ccatt
Primary use: Wernicke encephalopathy prevention/treatment; alcoholic patients; malnutrition; refeeding syndrome
Mechanism: Cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, transketolase → essential for glucose oxidation and ATP production; deficiency → lactic acidosis, neuronal dysfunction, and Wernicke encephalopathy; glucose administration in thiamine-deficient patients → worsens deficiency by accelerating thiamine-dependent glucose metabolism
WARNINGS: IV thiamine is SAFE — no reason to delay dextrose for thiamine (VA study 2025). Give together. Anaphylaxis rare with IV thiamine — resuscitation equipment available. Thiamine injections may cause injection site reactions.
Notes: Updated evidence: VA 10-year study (Jasti et al., Acad Emerg Med 2025) — WE from giving dextrose before thiamine is extremely rare. Do NOT delay hypoglycemia treatment for thiamine, but give both together whenever possible.

k: pancreatic hormone / glycogenolytic agent / beta-blocker antidote
chunks.x:
DRUG: Glucagon
Class: Pancreatic hormone / Glycogenolytic agent / Beta-blocker antidote
Category: electrolyte
Levels: r12, pfc, ccatt
Primary use: Hypoglycemia (no IV access); beta-blocker overdose; calcium channel blocker adjunct; esophageal food bolus
Mechanism: Glucagon receptor agonism → hepatic glycogenolysis + gluconeogenesis → glucose release; positive inotropy and chronotropy via cAMP (bypasses β-receptor → works in beta-blocker overdose); GI smooth muscle relaxation; requires intact hepatic glycogen stores for glucose effect

Notes: BB overdose dosing is 5-10× the hypoglycemia dose. Large doses required to overcome competitive antagonism. Expensive and short shelf life — but irreplaceable for BB/CCB OD when calcium + HDIE insufficient.
