chunks.x:
Glucagon for Beta-blocker overdose — bypasses blocked β-receptors
1 mg glucagon → cAMP pathway BYPASSES β1 receptors → positive inotropy and chronotropy even with complete β-blockade. 5-10 mg IV bolus; high doses required. Standard BB/CCB overdose protocol.

k: pancreatic hormone / glycogenolytic agent / beta-blocker antidote
chunks.x:
Glucagon for Hypoglycemia — no IV access (IM/SQ)
1 mg IM or SQ when IV unavailable. Requires intact hepatic glycogen → DOES NOT work in alcoholics, malnourished, prolonged fasting, or liver failure.

k: pancreatic hormone / glycogenolytic agent / beta-blocker antidote
chunks.x:
Glucagon for Esophageal food bolus impaction
1 mg IV/IM relaxes lower esophageal sphincter and esophageal smooth muscle → facilitates passage of food bolus impaction. Field-relevant when endoscopy unavailable.

k: pancreatic hormone / glycogenolytic agent / beta-blocker antidote
refractory bradycardia adjunct — calcium channel blocker od
chunks.x:
Glucagon for Refractory bradycardia adjunct — calcium channel blocker OD
CCB OD adjunct: glucagon positive chronotropy supplements calcium + HDIE protocol when bradycardia refractory.
chunks.u: Refractory bradycardia adjunct — calcium channel blocker OD

chunks.x:
DRUG: Labetalol / Nicardipine (Hypertensive Emergency)
Class: Alpha/Beta blocker (labetalol) / Dihydropyridine CCB (nicardipine) / Antihypertensive
Category: cardiac
Levels: pfc, ccatt
Primary use: Hypertensive emergency; hypertensive encephalopathy; aortic dissection; perioperative hypertension
Mechanism: Labetalol: combined α1 + non-selective β blockade → reduces SVR (α1) + HR/cardiac output (β) → smooth BP reduction without reflex tachycardia; Nicardipine: dihydropyridine calcium channel blockade → vascular smooth muscle relaxation → arterial vasodilation → BP reduction with preserved coronary flow
WARNINGS: Labetalol CONTRAINDICATED in asthma/COPD, decompensated heart failure, 2nd/3rd degree AV block. Nicardipine: reflex tachycardia possible; avoid in acute heart failure with poor LV function.
Notes: Target BP reduction: reduce MAP by max 25% in first hour → 160/100 over next 2-6h. Overly rapid reduction → cerebral, renal, coronary ischemia. Aortic dissection is the one exception — rapid aggressive reduction to SBP <120.

Labetalol / Nicardipine (Hypertensive Emergency) — PFC context: Severe hypertension from pain/anxiety/stimulant use. Post-TBI hypertension management. Aortic dissection BP control target SBP <120. IV labetalol 20 mg bolus.

Labetalol / Nicardipine (Hypertensive Emergency) — CCATT context: Full hypertensive emergency protocol. Nicardipine preferred for most hypertensive emergencies (titratable). Labetalol for aortic dissection, cocaine, hyperthyroidism. Avoid labetalol in asthma/COPD.

k: aortic dissection — rate and pressure control
chunks.x:
Labetalol / Nicardipine (Hypertensive Emergency) for Aortic dissection — rate and pressure control
Target HR <60 and SBP <120 mmHg. Labetalol first-line: reduces both HR and BP simultaneously. β-blockade before vasodilators to prevent reflex tachycardia from increasing aortic wall shear stress.
chunks.u: Aortic dissection — rate and pressure control

chunks.x:
Labetalol / Nicardipine (Hypertensive Emergency) for Cocaine/sympathomimetic hypertension — labetalol
Cocaine → sympathomimetic crisis → severe hypertension + tachycardia. Labetalol: combined α + β blockade manages both. Note: "pure beta-blocker" contraindicated in cocaine (unopposed α vasoconstriction).

Labetalol / Nicardipine (Hypertensive Emergency) for Post-TBI hypertension — controlled reduction
Hypertension after TBI may be Cushing response (ICP ↑) — treat underlying ICP first. When true hypertensive crisis: nicardipine preferred (titratable, no ICP effect).

Labetalol / Nicardipine (Hypertensive Emergency) for Perioperative hypertension — surgical BP control
Nicardipine 5-15 mg/hr IV for perioperative BP management; easily titratable; no negative inotropy.

k: extended-spectrum penicillin + beta-lactamase inhibitor / broad-spectrum bactericidal
chunks.x:
DRUG: Piperacillin-Tazobactam (Pip-Tazo / Zosyn)
Class: Extended-spectrum penicillin + beta-lactamase inhibitor / Broad-spectrum bactericidal
Category: abx
Levels: pfc, ccatt
Primary use: Healthcare-associated sepsis; necrotizing fasciitis; polymicrobial intraabdominal infections; Pseudomonas coverage
Mechanism: Piperacillin inhibits cell wall synthesis via PBP binding; tazobactam inhibits beta-lactamases → extends piperacillin spectrum to include beta-lactamase-producing organisms; covers gram-positive (except MRSA), gram-negative (including Pseudomonas), and anaerobes; IV only
WARNINGS: "Pip-tazo + vancomycin" combination: increased AKI risk (nephrotoxicity) compared to meropenem + vancomycin — monitor renal function closely. Hypokalemia common. Seizures at very high doses.
Notes: MERINO trial: pip-tazo inferior to meropenem for definitive treatment of ceftriaxone-resistant Enterobacteriaceae. Use pip-tazo empirically; escalate to meropenem if resistance confirmed.

k: extended-spectrum penicillin + beta-lactamase inhibitor / broad-spectrum bactericidal
chunks.x: Piperacillin-Tazobactam (Pip-Tazo / Zosyn) — PFC context: Severe polymicrobial wound infections. Necrotizing fasciitis surgical prophylaxis. Penetrating abdominal trauma with concern for hospital-acquired organisms. When ertapenem unavailable.

k: extended-spectrum penicillin + beta-lactamase inhibitor / broad-spectrum bactericidal
chunks.x: Piperacillin-Tazobactam (Pip-Tazo / Zosyn) — CCATT context: Healthcare-associated pneumonia (HAP/VAP). Febrile neutropenia. Sepsis empiric coverage. Severe intraabdominal infections. Add vancomycin for MRSA concern. Renal dose adjustment required.

k: extended-spectrum penicillin + beta-lactamase inhibitor / broad-spectrum bactericidal
chunks.x:
Piperacillin-Tazobactam (Pip-Tazo / Zosyn) for Necrotizing fasciitis — polymicrobial surgical prophylaxis
Pip-tazo + vancomycin = standard empiric coverage for necrotizing fasciitis (group A Strep, gram-negative rods, anaerobes). Broad spectrum covers all components.

k: extended-spectrum penicillin + beta-lactamase inhibitor / broad-spectrum bactericidal
chunks.x:
Piperacillin-Tazobactam (Pip-Tazo / Zosyn) for Pseudomonas coverage — burns, VAP, immunocompromised
One of few beta-lactams with Pseudomonas activity. Critical for burn casualties (Pseudomonas aeruginosa is leading burn pathogen) and ventilator-associated pneumonia.

k: extended-spectrum penicillin + beta-lactamase inhibitor / broad-spectrum bactericidal
chunks.x:
Piperacillin-Tazobactam (Pip-Tazo / Zosyn) for Febrile neutropenia — empiric monotherapy
Standard empiric monotherapy for febrile neutropenia in hemodynamically stable patients; broad-spectrum covers most likely pathogens.

DRUG: Loperamide (Imodium)
Class: Peripheral opioid receptor agonist / Antidiarrheal
Category: analgesia
Levels: r12, pfc
Primary use: Acute diarrhea; traveler's diarrhea; mission-degrading GI illness
Mechanism: Peripheral μ-opioid receptor agonism in GI tract → reduces intestinal motility and secretion → reduces stool frequency; does NOT cross BBB at therapeutic doses → no CNS opioid effects; also reduces gut permeability; OTC in most countries
WARNINGS: DO NOT USE with fever or bloody diarrhea (Shiga toxin-producing E. coli, C. diff, invasive pathogens — may worsen by slowing toxin clearance). Toxic megacolon risk if used in colitis. Overdose at high doses may cross BBB in children.
Notes: JTS guidance: loperamide for mild non-febrile non-bloody diarrhea; antibiotics (cipro/azithromycin) for moderate-severe, febrile, or bloody diarrhea. Never give both simultaneously — if sick enough for antibiotics, stop loperamide.

Loperamide (Imodium) — R12 context: Mission-degrading diarrhea in combat operations — 2 mg PO after each loose stool (max 16 mg/day). Allows mission continuation. Do NOT use with fever or bloody diarrhea (may worsen invasive bacterial GI infection).

Loperamide (Imodium) — PFC context: Standard kit item. Acute non-bloody, non-febrile diarrhea. Combine with oral rehydration solution. Reserve antibiotics (ciprofloxacin/azithromycin) for moderate-severe or febrile TD.

k: mission continuation — traveler's diarrhea symptom control
chunks.x:
Loperamide (Imodium) for Mission continuation — traveler's diarrhea symptom control
Reduces stool frequency 1.5-2× faster than placebo; allows combat mission continuation. OTC access means soldier can self-treat without medic consultation for mild diarrhea.
chunks.u: Mission continuation — traveler's diarrhea symptom control

k: chronic diarrhea management — prolonged field care
chunks.x:
Loperamide (Imodium) for Chronic diarrhea management — prolonged field care
For ongoing GI conditions in PFC: reduces fluid/electrolyte loss and maintains mission capacity when definitive diagnosis/treatment delayed.
chunks.u: Chronic diarrhea management — prolonged field care

k: short bowel syndrome / ileostomy output reduction
chunks.x:
Loperamide (Imodium) for Short bowel syndrome / ileostomy output reduction
High-output ileostomy or short bowel — loperamide reduces output significantly; relevant for post-surgical casualties in PFC.
chunks.u: Short bowel syndrome / ileostomy output reduction

k: synthetic catecholamine / selective β1 agonist / positive inotrope
chunks.x:
DRUG: Dobutamine
Class: Synthetic catecholamine / Selective β1 agonist / Positive inotrope
Category: vasoactive
Levels: ccatt
Primary use: Cardiogenic shock; acute decompensated heart failure with low output; cardiac dysfunction post-arrest
Mechanism: Selective β1 adrenergic agonism → positive inotropy + chronotropy → increases cardiac output; minimal α1 effect → does NOT increase SVR (unlike dopamine); mild β2 → slight vasodilation (reduces afterload); net effect: increased CO with reduced filling pressures; does NOT improve survival in ADHF but improves hemodynamics
WARNINGS: Arrhythmogenic — dose-dependent tachycardia and ectopy. Does NOT improve mortality in ADHF. Hypotension possible (β2 vasodilation). Central line preferred. Do NOT use in hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy.
Notes: Cardiogenic shock protocol: norepinephrine (maintains MAP) + dobutamine (improves CO). NE alone increases afterload worsening cardiogenic physiology; combination addresses both.

k: synthetic catecholamine / selective β1 agonist / positive inotrope
chunks.x: Dobutamine — CCATT context: Cardiogenic shock with low output despite adequate preload. Post-cardiac arrest myocardial stunning. Acute right heart failure. Dobutamine + norepinephrine combination for cardiogenic shock (NE maintains perfusion pressure; dobutamine increases CO).

k: synthetic catecholamine / selective β1 agonist / positive inotrope
chunks.x:
Dobutamine for Cardiogenic shock — inotropy without vasoconstriction
When cardiac output is critically low but SVR is already elevated (cardiogenic shock): dobutamine increases CO without raising SVR. Combines with NE to maintain MAP while dobutamine improves forward flow.

k: synthetic catecholamine / selective β1 agonist / positive inotrope
acute right heart failure — rv support
chunks.x:
Dobutamine for Acute right heart failure — RV support
RV failure from PE, ARDS, or cardiac contusion — dobutamine supports RV contractility; combination with vasopressin for RV failure-related shock.
chunks.u: Acute right heart failure — RV support

k: synthetic catecholamine / selective β1 agonist / positive inotrope
chunks.x:
Dobutamine for Post-cardiac arrest myocardial stunning
Post-ROSC myocardial dysfunction (stunning) → low output despite adequate rhythm. Dobutamine 2-10 mcg/kg/min improves cardiac output during recovery period.

k: synthetic catecholamine / selective β1 agonist / positive inotrope
chunks.x:
Dobutamine for Stress echocardiography (pharmacologic stress)
Low-dose dobutamine stress echocardiography for coronary artery disease evaluation in patients unable to exercise.

k: heparin antidote / positively charged protein / anticoagulation reversal
chunks.x:
DRUG: Protamine Sulfate
Class: Heparin antidote / Positively charged protein / Anticoagulation reversal
Category: hemostasis
Levels: pfc, ccatt
Primary use: Heparin reversal; post-cardiac surgery anticoagulation reversal; ECMO circuit anticoagulation reversal
Mechanism: Positively charged protein → binds negatively charged heparin → forms inactive stable complex → neutralizes heparin anticoagulant effect; 1 mg protamine neutralizes 100 units UFH; partial reversal of LMWH (60-75%); does NOT reverse DOACs; given IV slowly — rapid administration causes anaphylactoid reactions
WARNINGS: Rapid IV administration → anaphylactoid reaction (hypotension, bradycardia, bronchospasm) — give SLOWLY over 10 min. Excessive protamine → paradoxical anticoagulation (protamine itself has weak anticoagulant activity). History of fish allergy or prior protamine exposure = increased anaphylaxis risk.
Notes: Dosing caveat: if >30 min since heparin → reduce protamine dose (heparin cleared). Formula: protamine dose (mg) = heparin dose (units) × 0.01, adjusted for time elapsed.

k: heparin antidote / positively charged protein / anticoagulation reversal
chunks.x: Protamine Sulfate — PFC context: Heparin overdose reversal. Post-tourniquet anticoagulation (heparin given for ACS during CASEVAC needs reversal for surgery). 1 mg per 100 units UFH given in past 2-3 hours.

k: heparin antidote / positively charged protein / anticoagulation reversal
chunks.x: Protamine Sulfate — CCATT context: Post-cardiac surgery reversal. ECMO circuit anticoagulation reversal. Heparin overdose. Careful dosing: excessive protamine has anticoagulant effect paradoxically.

k: heparin antidote / positively charged protein / anticoagulation reversal
chunks.x:
Protamine Sulfate for Heparin overdose reversal — immediate
1 mg protamine per 100 units UFH (given within past 2-3h). Immediate neutralization. Essential for surgical casualty who received therapeutic heparin for ACS/DVT during CASEVAC.

k: heparin antidote / positively charged protein / anticoagulation reversal
chunks.x:
Protamine Sulfate for LMWH partial reversal (enoxaparin)
1 mg protamine per 1 mg enoxaparin given within 8h — reverses ~60-75% of anti-Xa activity. Partial but clinically meaningful reversal for bleeding complications.

k: heparin antidote / positively charged protein / anticoagulation reversal
chunks.x:
Protamine Sulfate for ECMO circuit anticoagulation management
Precise heparin reversal during ECMO cannula removal or circuit change. Dosing based on ACT/anti-Xa levels.

k: nucleoside analogue antiviral / herpesvirus dna polymerase inhibitor
chunks.x:
DRUG: Acyclovir (Zovirax)
Class: Nucleoside analogue antiviral / Herpesvirus DNA polymerase inhibitor
Category: abx
Levels: pfc, ccatt
Primary use: Herpes simplex encephalitis; severe varicella/zoster; herpes simplex keratitis; immunocompromised herpes
Mechanism: Converted by viral thymidine kinase to acyclovir monophosphate → further phosphorylated to acyclovir triphosphate → inhibits viral DNA polymerase → chain termination; selective for virus-infected cells (requires viral enzyme for activation); active against HSV-1, HSV-2, VZV; less active against EBV, CMV
WARNINGS: Nephrotoxicity — aggressive IV hydration required (1L NS before and after each dose). Crystalluria in dehydrated patients. Neurotoxicity (confusion, tremor) with high doses or renal failure. Renal dose adjustment essential.
Notes: HSE teaching: IV acyclovir must be started EMPIRICALLY in any patient with unexplained encephalitis — do not wait for PCR. Delay in treatment dramatically worsens outcomes. Untreated HSE mortality >70%; treated <20%.

k: nucleoside analogue antiviral / herpesvirus dna polymerase inhibitor
chunks.x: Acyclovir (Zovirax) — PFC context: Herpes simplex encephalitis (HSE) — life-threatening, treat empirically. Ocular herpes (keratitis) from blast/trauma causing corneal exposure. Severe varicella in adult deployed personnel.

k: nucleoside analogue antiviral / herpesvirus dna polymerase inhibitor
chunks.x: Acyclovir (Zovirax) — CCATT context: IV acyclovir 10 mg/kg q8h for HSE (14-21 days). VZV encephalitis, disseminated zoster. Immunocompromised herpes. Renal dose adjustment essential.

k: nucleoside analogue antiviral / herpesvirus dna polymerase inhibitor
chunks.x:
Acyclovir (Zovirax) for Herpes simplex encephalitis — empiric treatment
HSE is rapidly fatal without treatment; empiric IV acyclovir 10 mg/kg q8h started BEFORE PCR confirmation is standard of care. Diagnosis of exclusion — treat empirically in unexplained encephalitis.

k: nucleoside analogue antiviral / herpesvirus dna polymerase inhibitor
chunks.x:
Acyclovir (Zovirax) for Ocular herpes — blast/trauma corneal exposure
Blast trauma can cause corneal HSV reactivation via stress or direct inoculation. Acyclovir ophthalmic ointment or oral for dendritic corneal ulcer; IV for severe cases.

k: nucleoside analogue antiviral / herpesvirus dna polymerase inhibitor
varicella (chickenpox) in adults — severe disease prevention
chunks.x:
Acyclovir (Zovirax) for Varicella (chickenpox) in adults — severe disease prevention
Adult varicella has 25× higher complication rate than childhood disease. IV acyclovir for pneumonia, encephalitis, or severe disease in deployed immunocompetent adults.
chunks.u: Varicella (chickenpox) in adults — severe disease prevention

k: organic nitrate / nitric oxide donor / venodilator
chunks.x:
DRUG: Nitroglycerin (NTG / Nitro)
Class: Organic nitrate / Nitric oxide donor / Venodilator
Category: cardiac
Levels: pfc, ccatt
Primary use: Acute coronary syndrome; angina; acute pulmonary edema; hypertensive emergency with cardiac involvement
Mechanism: Metabolized to nitric oxide (NO) → activates guanylyl cyclase → ↑cGMP → smooth muscle dephosphorylation → relaxation; venodilation at low doses → preload reduction; arteriodilation at high doses → afterload reduction; coronary vasodilation → improved myocardial perfusion; onset SL: 1-3 min; IV: immediate; half-life: 1-3 min
WARNINGS: CONTRAINDICATED: SBP <90 mmHg; RV infarction (preload-dependent); phosphodiesterase inhibitors (sildenafil/tadalafil — severe hypotension). NTG alone in aortic dissection → reflex tachycardia → worsens dissection. Always beta-blocker first.
Notes: SCAPE protocol: IV NTG 1-2 mg bolus (much higher than standard ACS dose) rapidly relieves flash pulmonary edema. Tolerance develops with continuous infusion >12-24h — nitrate-free interval needed.

k: organic nitrate / nitric oxide donor / venodilator
chunks.x: Nitroglycerin (NTG / Nitro) — PFC context: ACS chest pain: 0.4 mg SL q5 min × 3 doses. Hypertensive pulmonary edema: SL bridge to IV. Available as tablet, spray, or IV. CONTRAINDICATED if SBP <90 or RV infarct.

k: organic nitrate / nitric oxide donor / venodilator
chunks.x: Nitroglycerin (NTG / Nitro) — CCATT context: IV NTG 10-200 mcg/min titrated for ACS, pulmonary edema, hypertensive emergency. Continuous BP monitoring essential. SCAPE (sympathetic crashing acute pulmonary edema): high-dose IV NTG 1-2 mg bolus.

k: organic nitrate / nitric oxide donor / venodilator
acs/stemi chest pain — coronary vasodilation + preload reduction
chunks.x:
Nitroglycerin (NTG / Nitro) for ACS/STEMI chest pain — coronary vasodilation + preload reduction
AHA/ACC Class I recommendation: up to 3 SL doses q5 min, then IV if needed. Reduces myocardial O2 demand + improves coronary flow. Early IV NTG in first 24-48h reduces infarct size.
chunks.u: ACS/STEMI chest pain — coronary vasodilation + preload reduction

k: scape (sympathetic crashing acute pulmonary edema) — high-dose ntg
organic nitrate / nitric oxide donor / venodilator
chunks.x:
Nitroglycerin (NTG / Nitro) for SCAPE (Sympathetic Crashing Acute Pulmonary Edema) — high-dose NTG
High-dose IV NTG 1-2 mg bolus for SCAPE (flash pulmonary edema with severe HTN) more effective than high-dose furosemide. Rapid preload + afterload reduction.
chunks.u: SCAPE (Sympathetic Crashing Acute Pulmonary Edema) — high-dose NTG

k: organic nitrate / nitric oxide donor / venodilator
chunks.x:
Nitroglycerin (NTG / Nitro) for Aortic dissection — BP/HR reduction adjunct
After beta-blocker (esmolol/labetalol), add NTG for additional BP control. Target SBP <120. NTG alone causes reflex tachycardia — ALWAYS pair with beta-blocker.

k: esophageal food bolus impaction — smooth muscle relaxation
organic nitrate / nitric oxide donor / venodilator
chunks.x:
Nitroglycerin (NTG / Nitro) for Esophageal food bolus impaction — smooth muscle relaxation
0.4 mg SL NTG relaxes lower esophageal sphincter; facilitates bolus passage. Alternative to glucagon in the field.
chunks.u: Esophageal food bolus impaction — smooth muscle relaxation

chunks.x:
DRUG: Artemether-Lumefantrine (Coartem) / Mefloquine
Class: Artemisinin combination therapy (ACT) / Antimalarial
Category: abx
Levels: r12, pfc, ccatt
Primary use: Uncomplicated Plasmodium falciparum malaria treatment; multi-drug resistant malaria; deployed tropical operations
Mechanism: Artemether: artemisinin derivative → endoperoxide bridge generates reactive oxygen species within parasite → kills intraerythrocytic parasites rapidly; lumefantrine: slowly-eliminated partner drug → kills remaining parasites and prevents recrudescence; together = rapid kill + sustained clearance; mefloquine: quinoline methanol → inhibits heme detoxification → toxic to blood-stage parasites
WARNINGS: Artemether-lumefantrine: take with food (fatty meal increases absorption 16-fold). QT prolongation — avoid with other QT-prolonging drugs. Mefloquine: CONTRAINDICATED in psychiatric history, seizures, cardiac conduction abnormalities; 9.6% US military have contraindications.
Notes: Military malaria prophylaxis current preference: doxycycline 100 mg daily > mefloquine 250 mg weekly (neuropsychiatric side effects) > atovaquone-proguanil. For treatment of confirmed malaria: ACT (artemether-lumefantrine) is WHO/CDC standard.

Artemether-Lumefantrine (Coartem) / Mefloquine — R12 context: Deployed personnel in malaria-endemic areas. Artemether-lumefantrine (Coartem) 6-dose regimen over 3 days for confirmed P. falciparum. UN peacekeeping forces: documented mefloquine resistance → switch to ACT.

Artemether-Lumefantrine (Coartem) / Mefloquine — PFC context: Standard treatment of deployed personnel with uncomplicated malaria. Mefloquine prophylaxis (250 mg weekly) for endemic areas — but 9.6% of US military personnel have contraindications (psychiatric history). Doxycycline preferred prophylaxis.
Artemether-Lumefantrine (Coartem) / Mefloquine — CCATT context: Severe malaria: IV artesunate (if available) or IM artemether. Transition to oral ACT when able. Cerebral malaria management.

k: treatment-resistant malaria — act superior to chloroquine/mefloquine alone
chunks.x:
Artemether-Lumefantrine (Coartem) / Mefloquine for Treatment-resistant malaria — ACT superior to chloroquine/mefloquine alone
WHO recommends ACT as first-line for uncomplicated P. falciparum globally. Artemether-lumefantrine 6-dose regimen: >95% cure rate in most settings. UN peacekeeping forces data: effective even when mefloquine prophylaxis fails.
chunks.u: Treatment-resistant malaria — ACT superior to chloroquine/mefloquine alone

chunks.x:
Artemether-Lumefantrine (Coartem) / Mefloquine for Mefloquine prophylaxis failure rescue treatment
When breakthrough malaria occurs on mefloquine prophylaxis, ACT (artemether-lumefantrine) is the treatment. Do NOT use mefloquine for treatment if used for prophylaxis in past 63 days.

Artemether-Lumefantrine (Coartem) / Mefloquine for Gametocyte clearance — reduces transmission
Artemisinin derivatives uniquely kill gametocytes (transmission stage) — reduces malaria spread among unit personnel in endemic areas.

DRUG: Aspirin (ASA)
Class: NSAID / Irreversible COX-1 inhibitor / Antiplatelet
Category: cardiac
Levels: r12, pfc, ccatt
Primary use: ACS/STEMI antiplatelet; stroke prevention; analgesia/antipyretic; Kawasaki disease
Mechanism: Irreversible acetylation of COX-1 → blocks thromboxane A2 synthesis → permanent platelet inhibition for platelet lifetime (7-10 days); platelet has no nucleus → cannot regenerate COX-1 → one dose provides 7-10 day antiplatelet effect; at higher doses: COX-2 inhibition → anti-inflammatory; prostaglandin inhibition → analgesia/antipyresis
WARNINGS: Contraindicated in active bleeding, hemorrhagic stroke, aspirin allergy. AVOID in suspected hemorrhagic TBI — platelet inhibition worsens intracranial bleeding. Reye syndrome in children <18 with viral illness.
Notes: ACS pearl: CHEW aspirin (do not swallow whole) — chewing provides 5× faster absorption and platelet inhibition vs swallowed tablet. This single point improves outcomes.

Aspirin (ASA) — R12 context: ACS protocol: 325 mg PO chewed (not swallowed — faster absorption). Every IFAK for chest pain protocol. Chewable aspirin in every aid bag — ACS NNT 10-42 (much better than NTG NNT 125-250).
Aspirin (ASA) — PFC context: Full ACS protocol. STEMI management. Ischemic stroke (non-hemorrhagic confirmed). Anti-inflammatory for mild-moderate pain.
Aspirin (ASA) — CCATT context: ACS loading dose + maintenance. Heparin + aspirin for ACS. Antiplatelet therapy continuation. Pericarditis anti-inflammatory.

Aspirin (ASA) for ACS — irreplaceable first-line antiplatelet
Chew 325 mg immediately in suspected ACS. NNT 10-42 — far superior to nitroglycerin (NNT 125-250) for ACS mortality reduction. AHA/ACC Class I. Must be chewed (not swallowed) for fastest absorption.

Aspirin (ASA) for Ischemic stroke — antithrombotic (non-hemorrhagic)
325 mg PO for acute ischemic stroke when thrombolytics not available or contraindicated. Confirm non-hemorrhagic (CT) before giving.

Aspirin (ASA) for Pericarditis — anti-inflammatory first-line
Aspirin 750-1000 mg TID × 1-2 weeks (with colchicine) is first-line for acute pericarditis treatment; superior to other NSAIDs per ESC guidelines.

Aspirin (ASA) for Fever reduction — combat zone antipyretic
650 mg PO q4-6h effective antipyretic; less platelet inhibition concern than in hemorrhagic setting; alternative to acetaminophen when unavailable.

k: mixed adrenergic agonist (indirect + direct) / vasopressor / bronchodilator
chunks.x:
DRUG: Ephedrine
Class: Mixed adrenergic agonist (indirect + direct) / Vasopressor / Bronchodilator
Category: vasoactive
Levels: pfc, ccatt
Primary use: Spinal/epidural anesthesia hypotension; mild bronchospasm; nasal decongestant; vasopressor bridge
Mechanism: Both direct adrenergic agonism (α and β) AND indirect (norepinephrine release from vesicles) → vasopressor + chronotropic + inotropic + bronchodilatory effects; oral bioavailability; crosses BBB → CNS stimulation; prolonged action vs epinephrine; tachyphylaxis with repeated dosing (norepinephrine depletion)
WARNINGS: Tachyphylaxis with repeated doses — norepinephrine stores depleted. Hypertension, tachycardia, arrhythmias. Avoid in hypertension, coronary artery disease, MAO inhibitor use (hypertensive crisis). CNS stimulation — insomnia, anxiety.
Notes: Obstetric spinal anesthesia: phenylephrine now preferred over ephedrine (less fetal acidosis). For general surgical spinal hypotension: ephedrine remains useful due to combined α+β effects maintaining both BP and HR.

k: mixed adrenergic agonist (indirect + direct) / vasopressor / bronchodilator
chunks.x: Ephedrine — PFC context: Spinal anesthesia hypotension in field surgery. Mild bronchospasm when albuterol unavailable. Hemodynamic support during induction. 5-25 mg IV/IM.

k: mixed adrenergic agonist (indirect + direct) / vasopressor / bronchodilator
chunks.x: Ephedrine — CCATT context: Anesthesia hypotension management. Alternative vasopressor when NE unavailable. Oral preparation available for mild bronchospasm management.

k: mixed adrenergic agonist (indirect + direct) / vasopressor / bronchodilator
chunks.x:
Ephedrine for Spinal anesthesia hypotension — first-line vasopressor
5-25 mg IV bolus for spinal anesthesia-induced hypotension. Unlike phenylephrine, ephedrine has both α1 (vasoconstriction) and β1 (inotropy/chronotropy) effects — maintains BP and HR.

k: mild bronchospasm — oral/im when nebulizer unavailable
mixed adrenergic agonist (indirect + direct) / vasopressor / bronchodilator
chunks.x:
Ephedrine for Mild bronchospasm — oral/IM when nebulizer unavailable
Bronchodilation via β2 agonism; less potent than albuterol but available PO/IM. Historical standard before albuterol availability.
chunks.u: Mild bronchospasm — oral/IM when nebulizer unavailable

k: mixed adrenergic agonist (indirect + direct) / vasopressor / bronchodilator
chunks.x:
Ephedrine for Vasopressor bridge — mild distributive shock
When NE/dopamine not yet available; 25-50 mg IM provides 15-30 min vasopressor support as bridge.

k: p2y12 adp receptor antagonist / antiplatelet / thienopyridine prodrug
chunks.x:
DRUG: Clopidogrel (Plavix)
Class: P2Y12 ADP receptor antagonist / Antiplatelet / Thienopyridine prodrug
Category: cardiac
Levels: pfc, ccatt
Primary use: ACS dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT); post-PCI stent protection; ischemic stroke secondary prevention
Mechanism: Prodrug → hepatic CYP2C19 activation → active metabolite irreversibly blocks P2Y12 ADP receptor on platelets → inhibits ADP-mediated platelet aggregation; additive with aspirin (different pathway) → dual antiplatelet therapy; onset 2-6h after loading dose (600 mg loading for ACS)
WARNINGS: Bleeding risk — especially with dual antiplatelet. CYP2C19 poor metabolizers (25% of some populations) — reduced efficacy. CONTRAINDICATED in active bleeding, hemorrhagic stroke. Do NOT combine with PPIs (omeprazole reduces clopidogrel activation).
Notes: CURE trial: clopidogrel + aspirin for NSTEMI — 20% relative risk reduction in CV death/MI/stroke. Military application: deployed personnel with known CAD on clopidogrel must continue — abrupt cessation → stent thrombosis within days.

k: p2y12 adp receptor antagonist / antiplatelet / thienopyridine prodrug
chunks.x: Clopidogrel (Plavix) — PFC context: ACS loading dose: 600 mg PO (or 300 mg) immediately. Aspirin + clopidogrel = DAPT standard. Ischemic stroke (non-hemorrhagic) antiplatelet.

k: p2y12 adp receptor antagonist / antiplatelet / thienopyridine prodrug
chunks.x: Clopidogrel (Plavix) — CCATT context: Full ACS management: DAPT with aspirin + clopidogrel or ticagrelor. Post-PCI stent protection continuation. PAD antiplatelet management during CASEVAC.

k: p2y12 adp receptor antagonist / antiplatelet / thienopyridine prodrug
acs — dapt with aspirin reduces mortality

DRUG: Hemostatic Dressings (QuikClot / Combat Gauze)
Class: Topical hemostatic agent / Kaolin-impregnated gauze / Chitosan dressing
Category: hemostasis
Levels: r12, pfc, ccatt
Primary use: Uncontrolled extremity hemorrhage where tourniquet not applicable; junctional wounds; wound packing
Mechanism: Combat Gauze (QuikClot): kaolin (aluminum silicate) activates factor XII → accelerates intrinsic coagulation cascade; does NOT generate heat (older zeolite did); must be applied with sustained direct pressure 3-5 min; Chitosan (HemCon): positively charged → attracts negatively charged RBCs → physical aggregation clot; WoundStat: pro-coagulant mineral (largely withdrawn due to thromboembolism concerns)

Notes: TCCC hemorrhage control hierarchy: direct pressure → tourniquet (extremity) → hemostatic gauze + pressure (junctional) → junctional tourniquet device. Combat Gauze is CoTCCC-approved hemostatic agent of choice.

chunks.x:
DRUG: Milrinone (Primacor)
Class: PDE3 inhibitor / Inodilator / Non-catecholamine positive inotrope
Category: vasoactive
Levels: ccatt
Primary use: Cardiogenic shock; right heart failure; pulmonary hypertension; beta-blocker OD inotropy
Mechanism: Inhibits phosphodiesterase-3 (PDE3) → ↑cAMP → ↑intracellular Ca²⁺ → positive inotropy + lusitropy; simultaneously vasodilates → reduces preload + afterload; mechanism BYPASSES β-receptors → effective even in beta-blocker toxicity or receptor downregulation; "inodilator" = inotropy + vasodilation
WARNINGS: Hypotension — dose-limiting; reduce if MAP falls. Arrhythmogenic. No reversal agent. Long half-life (2-3h) → slow offset. Renal dose adjustment required. Contraindicated in hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy.
Notes: KEY advantage over dobutamine: bypasses β-receptors → works in beta-blocker toxicity and receptor downregulation. DOREMI trial confirmed equivalence for cardiogenic shock — use milrinone when pulmonary HTN or BB OD concern.

k: specific doac reversal agents / monoclonal antibody fragment / modified factor xa decoy
chunks.x:
DRUG: Idarucizumab (Praxbind) / Andexanet Alfa (Andexxa)
Class: Specific DOAC reversal agents / Monoclonal antibody fragment / Modified factor Xa decoy
Category: hemostasis
Levels: pfc, ccatt
Primary use: Life-threatening bleeding in DOAC-anticoagulated casualties; emergency surgery requiring immediate hemostasis
Mechanism: Idarucizumab: humanized monoclonal antibody fragment → binds dabigatran (direct thrombin inhibitor) with 350× higher affinity than thrombin → immediate complete reversal; Andexanet alfa: modified recombinant inactive factor Xa → binds and sequesters factor Xa inhibitors (apixaban, rivaroxaban) → restores hemostasis; both work within minutes
WARNINGS: Idarucizumab: thrombotic events 4.8% at 30 days (restart anticoagulation ASAP when safe). Andexanet: infusion reactions 18%; anti-Xa returns to baseline ~2h after infusion ends (monitor for rebound). Both extremely expensive.
Notes: Drug-specific matching: dabigatran (Pradaxa) → idarucizumab; apixaban (Eliquis)/rivaroxaban (Xarelto) → andexanet alfa. If agent unknown: 4F-PCC as bridge. ISTH 2024: specific agents preferred over PCC when available.

DRUG: Cryoprecipitate / Fibrinogen Concentrate
Class: Blood product / Fibrinogen + Factor VIII + vWF + Factor XIII source
Category: hemostasis
Levels: pfc, ccatt
Primary use: Fibrinogen deficiency; coagulopathy; massive transfusion; DIC; TBI coagulopathy
Mechanism: Cryoprecipitate: cold-precipitated plasma fraction → concentrated fibrinogen (factor I), factor VIII, von Willebrand factor (vWF), factor XIII, fibronectin; fibrinogen is the most consumed coagulation factor in massive hemorrhage and DIC; target fibrinogen >150-200 mg/dL in trauma coagulopathy

DRUG: Primaquine / Tafenoquine
Class: 8-aminoquinoline antimalarial / Hypnozoite eradicator / Gametocytocidal
Category: abx
Levels: pfc
Primary use: Radical cure of P. vivax and P. ovale malaria (liver hypnozoite eradication); malaria transmission prevention
Mechanism: 8-aminoquinoline → oxidative stress in parasite mitochondria → kills liver-stage hypnozoites (dormant P. vivax/ovale forms) AND gametocytes; ONLY class that eradicates hypnozoites → prevents relapsing malaria; primaquine requires G6PD testing before use (hemolytic anemia in G6PD deficiency)
WARNINGS: G6PD TESTING MANDATORY before primaquine — G6PD deficiency causes life-threatening hemolytic anemia. Contraindicated in pregnancy (fetal G6PD unknown). Common in African, Mediterranean, Southeast Asian personnel (up to 25% prevalence).
Notes: Afghanistan deployment: P. vivax is primary malaria species. Without primaquine radical cure, returning personnel relapse months after homecoming. All P. vivax cases must receive primaquine after G6PD screening.

Primaquine / Tafenoquine — PFC context: Radical cure after P. vivax/ovale treatment — add primaquine 30 mg PO daily × 14 days after chloroquine or ACT. Afghanistan/tropical deployments: P. vivax is primary species — without primaquine, 50% relapse within months. G6PD testing MANDATORY first.

DRUG: Colchicine
Class: Alkaloid anti-inflammatory / Microtubule inhibitor / Neutrophil migration inhibitor
Category: antiinflam
Levels: pfc, ccatt

DRUG: Sodium Nitroprusside (Nipride)
Class: Vasodilator / Nitric oxide donor / Most potent titratable antihypertensive
Category: vasoactive
Levels: ccatt
Primary use: Hypertensive emergency refractory to other agents; controlled hypotension; acute heart failure afterload reduction
Mechanism: Spontaneous release of nitric oxide → direct arteriolar AND venous vasodilation → reduces both preload and afterload; most potent and titratable IV antihypertensive available; onset immediate; offset 1-2 min after stopping; metabolized to cyanide → thiocyanate (CN toxicity with prolonged high-dose use)

Mechanism: Atovaquone: inhibits mitochondrial cytochrome bc1 complex → disrupts parasite electron transport → depletes ATP; proguanil (DHFR inhibitor) potentiates atovaquone synergistically; no neuropsychiatric side effects; start 1-2 days before travel (vs 2-3 weeks for mefloquine)
WARNINGS: Take with food — fatty meal increases absorption 3x; without food bioavailability severely reduced. Cannot eradicate P. vivax/ovale hypnozoites — add primaquine for radical cure. Renal insufficiency: avoid if CrCl <30 mL/min. Expensive vs doxycycline.
Notes: Military prophylaxis decision tree: doxycycline (cheapest, broadest) > atovaquone-proguanil (no neuropsychiatric, flexible start) > mefloquine (weekly, but 9.6% contraindication rate). Atovaquone-proguanil preferred for personnel with psychiatric history or short-notice deployment.

k: who ors / glucose-sodium cotransport-based rehydration / electrolyte replacement
chunks.x:
DRUG: Oral Rehydration Salts (ORS) / Electrolyte Replacement
Class: WHO ORS / Glucose-sodium cotransport-based rehydration / Electrolyte replacement
Category: electrolyte
Levels: r12, pfc
Primary use: Dehydration from diarrhea or heat; electrolyte replacement without IV; heat casualty first-line
Mechanism: Glucose-sodium cotransport (SGLT1) in intestinal epithelium drives Na+ and water absorption even during active diarrhea; WHO ORS composition matched to intestinal fluid osmolarity; oral route effective even in moderate dehydration; avoids IV line complications; conserves IV supplies
WARNINGS: NOT for heat STROKE (altered mental status) — IV fluids and active cooling required. NOT for severe dehydration with vomiting. Plain water WITHOUT electrolytes can worsen hyponatremia in heat illness — always use ORS or add electrolytes.
Notes: WHO ORS formula: glucose 13.5 g/L + NaCl 2.6 g/L + KCl 1.5 g/L + sodium citrate 2.9 g/L. Field improvised: 1L clean water + 6 tsp sugar + half tsp salt = approximate ORS. Better than plain IV saline for mild-moderate dehydration.

chunks.x: Oral Rehydration Salts (ORS) / Electrolyte Replacement — R12 context: Heat casualties with mild-moderate dehydration (alert, able to drink): aggressive ORS 1-2L first hour. Diarrheal illness dehydration. Electrolyte replacement post-exercise. Always oral first when patient can drink.

k: who ors / glucose-sodium cotransport-based rehydration / electrolyte replacement
chunks.x: Oral Rehydration Salts (ORS) / Electrolyte Replacement — PFC context: Primary rehydration for patients without IV access. Heat exhaustion. Oral electrolytes during PFC when IV supply limited. Supplement or replace IV therapy in cooperative patients.

chunks.x:

chunks.x:
Oral Rehydration Salts (ORS) / Electrolyte Replacement for Diarrheal illness — prevents 80% of IV fluid needs

k: long-acting benzodiazepine / gaba-a modulator / muscle relaxant
chunks.x:
DRUG: Diazepam (Valium)
Class: Long-acting benzodiazepine / GABA-A modulator / Muscle relaxant
Category: analgesia
Levels: r12, pfc, ccatt
Primary use: Seizure rescue (rectal route); alcohol withdrawal; muscle spasm; tetanus; procedural sedation
Mechanism: Positive allosteric GABA-A receptor modulation → enhanced Cl- influx → CNS depression; long half-life (20-100h) + active metabolite desmethyldiazepam (half-life 36-200h) → prolonged effect useful for alcohol withdrawal self-taper; rectal gel (Diastat) enables field seizure rescue without IV; IM absorption erratic unlike midazolam
WARNINGS: Erratic IM absorption — do NOT use IM diazepam for acute seizures (use midazolam IM instead). Very long half-life → accumulation in elderly and hepatic failure. Respiratory depression with opioids. Paradoxical agitation in elderly.
Notes: Tetanus teaching: BZDs are the cornerstone of tetanus spasm management. Doses of 10-40 mg/hr diazepam infusion may be needed for severe tetanus. Deployed tropical areas with poor vaccination coverage — tetanus is a real threat.

chunks.x: Diazepam (Valium) — R12 context: Seizure rescue — diazepam rectal gel 10-20 mg PR when no IV. IV 10 mg slowly for SE. Muscle spasm from combat injuries.

chunks.x: Diazepam (Valium) — PFC context: Alcohol/BZD withdrawal CIWA protocol. Muscle spasm in PFC. Rectal route for field seizures without IV. Tetanus spasm management.

chunks.x:

chunks.x:
Diazepam (Valium) for Tetanus — massive muscle spasm management
Tetanus requires very high BZD doses for spasm control; diazepam IV infusion (continuous high doses) for tetanic spasms. Deployed tropical areas with poor vaccination: tetanus remains relevant.

chunks.x:

k: micronutrient supplements / wound healing cofactors / immune support
chunks.x:
DRUG: Zinc / Vitamin C / PFC Micronutrients
Class: Micronutrient supplements / Wound healing cofactors / Immune support
Category: electrolyte
Levels: pfc
Primary use: Wound healing optimization in prolonged field care; immune support; scurvy prevention in extended isolation
Mechanism: Zinc: cofactor for >300 enzymes including wound healing metalloproteases, DNA polymerase, immune function; deficiency impairs wound healing and immune response within days of depletion. Vitamin C: essential for collagen synthesis (hydroxylation of proline and lysine); antioxidant; immune support; deficiency causes scurvy within 4-6 weeks of complete deprivation
WARNINGS: Zinc excess over 40 mg/day causes copper deficiency (neurological complications with prolonged high-dose zinc). Vitamin C over 2g/day causes oxalate kidney stones in predisposed individuals. Iron absorption reduced by zinc supplementation.
Notes: PFC nutrition teaching: after 72h of field care, micronutrients become clinically relevant for wound healing. Zinc + Vitamin C are most evidence-supported. Simple, cheap, and available in most field medical kits.

k: micronutrient supplements / wound healing cofactors / immune support
chunks.x: Zinc / Vitamin C / PFC Micronutrients — PFC context: PFC >72h: supplement zinc 220 mg PO daily + vitamin C 500-1000 mg PO daily. Combat wound healing optimization. Extended isolation or siege scenarios.

k: wound healing optimization in prolonged field care
micronutrient supplements / wound healing cofactors / immune support
chunks.x:
Zinc / Vitamin C / PFC Micronutrients for Wound healing optimization in prolonged field care
Zinc 220 mg + Vitamin C 500 mg daily during PFC promotes wound healing. Zinc and ascorbate deficiency impairs wound healing by 40-50% (surgical nutrition literature). Critical after 72h of field care.

chunks.x:

scurvy prevention in extended isolation or siege

Zinc / Vitamin C / PFC Micronutrients for Scurvy prevention in extended isolation or siege

Prolonged septic shock depletes endogenous vasopressin stores. Adding vasopressin 0.03 units/min to norepinephrine restores V1-mediated tone. VASST trial: equivalent to high-dose NE; spares catecholamines.

chunks.x:

40 units IV x1 may substitute for one dose of epinephrine in ACLS algorithm. V1-mediated vasoconstriction maintains coronary and cerebral perfusion pressure during CPR.

k: synthetic vasopressin analogue / selective v2 agonist / hemostatic agent
chunks.x:
DRUG: Desmopressin (DDAVP)
Class: Synthetic vasopressin analogue / Selective V2 agonist / Hemostatic agent
Category: hemostasis
Levels: pfc, ccatt
Primary use: Central diabetes insipidus; mild hemophilia A; von Willebrand disease; uremic bleeding; platelet dysfunction
Mechanism: Selective V2 receptor agonism → renal tubular water reabsorption (antidiuretic); also releases vWF and factor VIII from endothelial Weibel-Palade bodies → transiently increases vWF and factor VIII 2-5x → hemostatic effect; no V1 vasoconstriction; short-acting (4-8h)
WARNINGS: Hyponatremia with repeat dosing — monitor serum Na after each dose; hold if Na <130. Tachyphylaxis with repeated dosing (vWF/FVIII stores depleted after 2-3 doses — wait 24-48h). Avoid in severe CAD (V2-mediated thrombus risk).
Notes: DI post-TBI rule: urine output >250 mL/hr + urine specific gravity <1.005 + rising serum Na = central DI → desmopressin 1 mcg IV/SQ. Do NOT give plain water or hypotonic fluids without desmopressin — will not correct central DI.

k: synthetic vasopressin analogue / selective v2 agonist / hemostatic agent
chunks.x: Desmopressin (DDAVP) — PFC context: Central DI post-TBI: 1-4 mcg IV/SQ/IN x1 (monitor serum Na). Mild hemophilia A or vWD: 0.3 mcg/kg IV over 20 min pre-procedure. Uremic platelet dysfunction.

k: synthetic vasopressin analogue / selective v2 agonist / hemostatic agent
chunks.x: Desmopressin (DDAVP) — CCATT context: Central DI management during CASEVAC. Pre-procedural hemostasis in mild hemophilia A. Platelet dysfunction reversal (uremia, aspirin, antiplatelet agents).

k: synthetic vasopressin analogue / selective v2 agonist / hemostatic agent
chunks.x:
Desmopressin (DDAVP) for Central diabetes insipidus — TBI/pituitary injury
Post-TBI or post-neurosurgery central DI: urine output >250 mL/hr + rising Na. Desmopressin 1-4 mcg IV/SQ corrects water loss. Preferred over vasopressin for DI (no vasoconstriction).

k: synthetic vasopressin analogue / selective v2 agonist / hemostatic agent
mild hemophilia a and vwd — releases stored vwf/fviii
chunks.x:
Desmopressin (DDAVP) for Mild hemophilia A and vWD — releases stored vWF/FVIII
0.3 mcg/kg IV over 20 min: releases vWF and factor VIII from endothelium → 2-5x increase → adequate hemostasis for minor procedures or bleeding. Avoids blood products.

chunks.x:
Desmopressin (DDAVP) for Uremic platelet dysfunction — field hemostasis
Uremia impairs platelet adhesion; desmopressin 0.3 mcg/kg IV transiently corrects platelet dysfunction in uremic casualties. Relevant for renal failure with active bleeding.

chunks.x:
Desmopressin (DDAVP) for Antiplatelet agent reversal — aspirin/clopidogrel effect
Desmopressin partially reverses antiplatelet effects via vWF release and platelet activation; used pre-emergent surgery in antiplatelet-treated patients.

endogenous catecholamine / alpha-1 dominant + beta-1 agonist / first-line vasopressor
chunks.x:
Norepinephrine (Levophed) — Detailed Protocol for Septic shock — first-line vasopressor (SOAP II trial)
SOAP II trial (NEJM 2010): norepinephrine superior to dopamine for septic shock — lower mortality and fewer arrhythmias. Standard: norepinephrine 0.1-3 mcg/kg/min IV titrate to MAP 65.

endogenous catecholamine / alpha-1 dominant + beta-1 agonist / first-line vasopressor
chunks.x:
Norepinephrine (Levophed) — Detailed Protocol for Neurogenic shock — vasopressor for spinal cord injury
Spinal cord injury above T6 → sympathetic outflow loss → distributive shock; unlike hemorrhagic shock, fluid alone insufficient; norepinephrine maintains MAP and spinal cord perfusion pressure.

When central venous access unavailable: peripheral NE 8-16 mcg/mL concentration acceptable for short-term use (<24h, large antecubital vein). Check for extravasation q30 min — treat with phentolamine if occurs.

k: first-generation cephalosporin / beta-lactam / cell wall synthesis inhibitor
chunks.x:
DRUG: Cefazolin (Ancef)
Class: First-generation cephalosporin / Beta-lactam / Cell wall synthesis inhibitor
Category: abx
Levels: pfc, ccatt
Primary use: Surgical prophylaxis; MSSA skin/soft tissue infections; orthopedic/wound prophylaxis; penicillin-sensitive gram-positive infections
Mechanism: Beta-lactam inhibits PBP3 (transpeptidase) → prevents cell wall crosslinking → bactericidal; first-generation cephalosporin → excellent gram-positive coverage (MSSA, streptococci) + limited gram-negative coverage; penetrates bone well → orthopedic infections; IV/IM; most commonly used surgical prophylaxis antibiotic in US military
WARNINGS: Cross-reactivity with penicillin allergy: ~1% if rash history, ~0.01% if no history. If history of anaphylaxis to penicillin: use vancomycin instead. Renal dose adjustment required. C. diff risk lower than broader antibiotics.
Notes: Surgical prophylaxis teaching: cefazolin 2g IV within 60 min before incision — not earlier, not after. Redose every 4h for prolonged surgery. MRSA-endemic facility: add vancomycin. Obese patients (>120 kg): 3g dose.

k: first-generation cephalosporin / beta-lactam / cell wall synthesis inhibitor
chunks.x: Cefazolin (Ancef) — PFC context: Surgical wound prophylaxis: 2g IV within 60 min before incision. MSSA wound infections. Orthopedic injuries (fractures, joint wounds). Penicillin-allergic alternative assessment.

k: first-generation cephalosporin / beta-lactam / cell wall synthesis inhibitor
chunks.x: Cefazolin (Ancef) — CCATT context: Pre-operative prophylaxis for all surgical procedures. MSSA bacteremia. Bone and joint infections. 2g IV q8h for serious infections. Adjust for renal function.

k: surgical prophylaxis — most used military perioperative antibiotic
first-generation cephalosporin / beta-lactam / cell wall synthesis inhibitor
chunks.x:
Cefazolin (Ancef) for Surgical prophylaxis — most used military perioperative antibiotic
2g IV within 60 min of incision; redose every 4h if surgery prolonged. Covers MSSA (most common surgical wound pathogen). Standard for clean and clean-contaminated procedures.
chunks.u: Surgical prophylaxis — most used military perioperative antibiotic

k: mssa bone and joint infections — excellent bone penetration
first-generation cephalosporin / beta-lactam / cell wall synthesis inhibitor
chunks.x:
Cefazolin (Ancef) for MSSA bone and joint infections — excellent bone penetration
Cefazolin penetrates bone well → preferred for MSSA osteomyelitis and septic arthritis. MSSA combat wound infections with bone involvement.
chunks.u: MSSA bone and joint infections — excellent bone penetration

k: first-generation cephalosporin / beta-lactam / cell wall synthesis inhibitor
chunks.x:
Cefazolin (Ancef) for Penicillin allergy — cross-reactivity assessment
Patients with penicillin allergy: if reaction was rash (not anaphylaxis), cefazolin cross-reactivity is <1% — can usually use. If anaphylaxis: avoid cefazolin, use vancomycin.

k: first-generation cephalosporin / beta-lactam / cell wall synthesis inhibitor
chunks.x:
Cefazolin (Ancef) for Streptococcal soft tissue infections
Strep pyogenes (Group A Strep) wound infections — cefazolin is highly effective; easier dosing than penicillin for serious infections.

chunks.x: Adenosine (Adenocard) — Extended Protocol — CCATT context: Full SVT protocol. Diagnostic tool for wide-complex tachycardia. NOT for AFib/flutter, ventricular tachycardia, or WPW with irregular rapid rhythm.

chunks.x:
Adenosine (Adenocard) — Extended Protocol for SVT termination — rapid IV push
6 mg rapid IV push (1-2 sec) followed by 20 mL NS flush immediately. If no effect in 2 min: 12 mg. Terminates most AVNRT and AVRT within 20 sec. Success rate 90%+.

endogenous nucleoside / av nodal blocker / svt terminator
chunks.x:
Adenosine (Adenocard) — Extended Protocol for Diagnostic tool — reveals atrial flutter waves
6 mg IV transiently slows AV conduction → unmasks saw-tooth flutter waves on ECG obscured by ventricular rate. Differentiates AFL from AFib and SVT.

k: endogenous nucleoside / av nodal blocker / svt terminator
chunks.x:
Adenosine (Adenocard) — Extended Protocol for Wide-complex tachycardia differentiation
If stable wide-complex tachycardia converts with adenosine → it was SVT with aberrancy (not VT). If no conversion: likely VT or pre-excitation. Diagnostic information guides further management.

chunks.d: Potassium Chloride / Magnesium Sulfate IV (Electrolyte Replacement)
k: potassium chloride / magnesium sulfate iv (electrolyte replacement)
chunks.x:
DRUG: Potassium Chloride / Magnesium Sulfate IV (Electrolyte Replacement)
Class: Essential electrolyte replacement / Antiarrhythmic cofactor
Category: electrolyte
Levels: pfc, ccatt
Primary use: Hypokalemia; hypomagnesemia; cardiac arrhythmia prevention; refeeding syndrome; diuretic-induced electrolyte loss
Mechanism: K+ essential for resting membrane potential (Nernst equation); hypokalemia → membrane hyperpolarization → cardiac arrhythmia risk; Mg2+ cofactor for Na/K-ATPase → hypomagnesemia causes refractory hypokalemia; replace Mg first or simultaneously with K+ or K+ replacement will be ineffective; critical post-diuretic and post-resuscitation
WARNINGS: NEVER give K+ IV push or rapid IV bolus — fatal cardiac arrhythmias. Max rate KCl: 10-20 mEq/hr peripheral, 40 mEq/hr central with monitoring. K+ concentration max 80 mEq/L peripheral. ALWAYS replace Mg simultaneously with K+ replacement.
Notes: Rule: always replace Mg2+ before or with K+ in any serious hypokalemia. You cannot adequately replace K+ with concurrent hypomagnesemia — Na/K-ATPase is Mg-dependent and will not work without it.

chunks.d: Potassium Chloride / Magnesium Sulfate IV (Electrolyte Replacement)
k: potassium chloride / magnesium sulfate iv (electrolyte replacement)
chunks.x: Potassium Chloride / Magnesium Sulfate IV (Electrolyte Replacement) — PFC context: Post-massive transfusion: hypokalemia from citrate chelation. Post-furosemide diuresis. Cardiac arrhythmia prevention. KCl 40 mEq in 100 mL over 1h IV. Always replace Mg simultaneously.

chunks.d: Potassium Chloride / Magnesium Sulfate IV (Electrolyte Replacement)
k: potassium chloride / magnesium sulfate iv (electrolyte replacement)
chunks.x: Potassium Chloride / Magnesium Sulfate IV (Electrolyte Replacement) — CCATT context: Full electrolyte management. Citrate toxicity during MTP depletes ionized Ca and Mg. Refeeding syndrome protocol. TdP/QTc prolongation: MgSO4 2g IV first. Monitor K+, Mg2+, Ca2+ after every 4 units of pRBC in MTP.

chunks.d: Potassium Chloride / Magnesium Sulfate IV (Electrolyte Replacement)
k: potassium chloride / magnesium sulfate iv (electrolyte replacement)
chunks.x:
Potassium Chloride / Magnesium Sulfate IV (Electrolyte Replacement) for Post-MTP hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia
Massive transfusion: citrate in stored blood chelates Ca2+ and Mg2+ → hypomagnesemia → refractory hypokalemia. Replace Mg2+ first, then K+. Monitor every 4 units of pRBC during MTP.

chunks.d: Potassium Chloride / Magnesium Sulfate IV (Electrolyte Replacement)
k: potassium chloride / magnesium sulfate iv (electrolyte replacement)
chunks.x:
Potassium Chloride / Magnesium Sulfate IV (Electrolyte Replacement) for Refractory hypokalemia — treat hypomagnesemia first
Hypokalemia refractory to K+ replacement: almost always due to concurrent hypomagnesemia. Mg2+ is required for Na/K-ATPase function. Replace MgSO4 2-4g IV first, then K+ replacement will be effective.

chunks.d: Potassium Chloride / Magnesium Sulfate IV (Electrolyte Replacement)

potassium chloride / magnesium sulfate iv (electrolyte replacement)

Potassium Chloride / Magnesium Sulfate IV (Electrolyte Replacement) for Torsades de pointes / QTc prolongation — MgSO4
TdP (polymorphic VT): MgSO4 2g IV over 2 min → terminates and prevents recurrence. Also for QTc >500 ms or TdP risk from medications. Standard emergency antiarrhythmic.

Potassium Chloride / Magnesium Sulfate IV (Electrolyte Replacement) for Refeeding syndrome prevention — electrolyte monitoring
Refeeding after starvation → cellular uptake of K+, Mg2+, phosphate → severe hypokalemia and hypophosphatemia → cardiac arrhythmias and respiratory failure. Aggressive electrolyte replacement and monitoring required.

k: depolarizing neuromuscular blocker / nicotinic ach receptor agonist
chunks.x:
DRUG: Succinylcholine (Anectine / Suxamethonium)
Class: Depolarizing neuromuscular blocker / Nicotinic ACh receptor agonist
Category: airway
Levels: pfc, ccatt
Primary use: RSI paralysis (ultra-fast onset and offset); laryngospasm; full-stomach intubation; cannot-wait airway
Mechanism: Binds nicotinic ACh receptors → sustained depolarization → initial fasciculations then flaccid paralysis; metabolized by plasma pseudocholinesterase → 5-7 min duration (shortest of all NMBs); onset 45-60 sec IV; NO reversal agent (must wait for spontaneous recovery); depolarization causes K+ efflux → normal rise ~0.5 mEq/L; upregulated extrajunctional receptors (denervation, burns, immobilization) → massive K+ efflux → fatal hyperkalemia
WARNINGS: HYPERKALEMIA CONTRAINDICATIONS: burns >24-72h post-injury, spinal cord injury, stroke, prolonged immobilization, denervation, crush injury >72h — upregulated extrajunctional AChRs cause massive K+ release → fatal cardiac arrest. Safe within FIRST 24h of injury. Malignant hyperthermia trigger. Pseudocholinesterase deficiency → hours-long paralysis. FDA Black Box: do NOT use in children except emergency airway.
Notes: Succinylcholine vs rocuronium decision: use succinylcholine when (1) crash airway with no time, (2) no CICO concern, (3) no hyperkalemia risk factors, (4) sugammadex unavailable. Use rocuronium when (1) CICO risk exists, (2) hyperkalemia risk, (3) sugammadex available. If rocuronium without sugammadex — you CANNOT safely rescue a failed airway.

k: phenothiazine dye / redox agent / sgc inhibitor / methemoglobin reductase cofactor
chunks.x:
DRUG: Methylene Blue
Class: Phenothiazine dye / Redox agent / sGC inhibitor / Methemoglobin reductase cofactor
Category: antidote
Levels: pfc, ccatt
Primary use: Methemoglobinemia (FDA-approved); refractory vasoplegic / distributive shock; dapsone toxicity
Mechanism: Methemoglobinemia: acts as an electron carrier → reduces methemoglobin (Fe³⁺) back to functional hemoglobin (Fe²⁺) via NADPH-methemoglobin reductase. Vasoplegic shock: inhibits soluble guanylate cyclase (sGC) and nitric oxide synthase (NOS) → attenuates the NO–cGMP vasodilation pathway → restores vascular tone and catecholamine responsiveness. The single NO–cGMP target links the methemoglobinemia antidote role and the vasoplegia rescue role.
WARNINGS: CONTRAINDICATED in G6PD deficiency — causes hemolytic anemia (and paradoxically cannot reduce methemoglobin without G6PD). Serotonin syndrome risk when combined with serotonergic drugs (SSRIs, MAOIs, linezolid). Colors urine/skin blue — warn patient. High doses (>4 mg/kg) paradoxically CAUSE methemoglobinemia. Vasoplegia use is not TCCC-endorsed and does not replace standard fluid resuscitation and first-line vasopressors.
Notes: Dapsone–malaria-prophylaxis connection: G6PD-deficient personnel can develop methemoglobinemia from dapsone AND cannot receive methylene blue — screen G6PD before prescribing dapsone. Mechanistic dual-use example: the NO–cGMP target links the methemoglobinemia antidote role to vasoplegia rescue. Vasoplegia evidence is strongest in post-CPB syndrome (moderate) and weaker elsewhere — tiered and src-tagged accordingly.

Category: airway
Levels: pfc, ccatt
Primary use: RSI (rocuronium); prolonged neuromuscular blockade for ICU; facilitated intubation when succinylcholine contraindicated

k: triazole antifungal / ergosterol synthesis inhibitor / broad-spectrum mold and yeast coverage
chunks.x:
DRUG: Voriconazole (Vfend) / Antifungals
Class: Triazole antifungal / Ergosterol synthesis inhibitor / Broad-spectrum mold and yeast coverage
Category: abx
Levels: pfc, ccatt
Primary use: Invasive aspergillosis first-line; candidemia; Fusarium; immunocompromised fungal infections
Mechanism: Inhibits fungal CYP51 (14-alpha-lanosterol demethylase) → blocks ergosterol synthesis → disrupts fungal cell membrane integrity; broader spectrum than fluconazole — covers molds (Aspergillus, Fusarium) + yeasts (Candida including fluconazole-resistant); IV and oral formulations; oral bioavailability 96%; crosses blood-brain barrier

k: gi adsorbent / decontamination agent / non-specific toxin binder
chunks.x:
DRUG: Activated Charcoal (AC)
Class: GI adsorbent / Decontamination agent / Non-specific toxin binder
Category: antidote
Levels: pfc, ccatt
Primary use: Oral overdose GI decontamination within 1-2h; multi-dose enhanced elimination; CBRN oral toxin exposure
Mechanism: Highly porous carbon structure (800-1200 m2/g surface area) → non-specific adsorption of organic molecules via van der Waals forces → prevents GI absorption; single-dose within 1h reduces drug absorption by 40-90%; multi-dose activated charcoal (MDAC) enhances elimination via enterohepatic/entero-enteric recirculation interruption; does NOT absorb metals (iron, lithium), alcohols, or simple ions
WARNINGS: CONTRAINDICATED in: unprotected airway (aspiration risk — intubate first), decreased GI motility/obstruction, caustic ingestion. Does NOT absorb: iron, lithium, alcohols, simple electrolytes, cyanide. Do NOT give with sorbitol (severe electrolyte disturbances). Aspiration pneumonitis is the major risk — protect airway first.
Notes: 1-hour rule: most effective within 1h of ingestion, but STILL beneficial at 2-4h for slow-absorbing drugs (aspirin, extended-release formulations). Rule: if airway is protected and no contraindication, give charcoal for any significant oral overdose within 2h — judgment call beyond 2h.

k: non-selective alpha-adrenergic blocker / ne extravasation antidote / vasodilator
chunks.x:
DRUG: Phentolamine (Regitine)
Class: Non-selective alpha-adrenergic blocker / NE extravasation antidote / Vasodilator
Category: antidote
Levels: pfc, ccatt
Primary use: Norepinephrine/vasopressor extravasation antidote; hypertensive crisis from MAO inhibitor interaction; pheochromocytoma crisis; cocaine-induced hypertension
Mechanism: Non-selective alpha-1 and alpha-2 blockade → peripheral vasodilation; reverses local vasoconstriction from extravasated vasopressors (NE, dopamine, epinephrine) → prevents tissue necrosis; for hypertensive crises: systemic alpha blockade → rapid BP reduction; onset 1-2 min IV; duration 10-15 min
WARNINGS: Hypotension — have fluid bolus ready. Reflex tachycardia. Myocardial infarction trigger in CAD patients (demand increase from tachycardia). CRITICAL: peripheral vasopressor protocol — every unit administering peripheral NE must have phentolamine immediately available and staff trained in extravasation recognition.
Notes: NE extravasation protocol: check site every 30 minutes during peripheral NE infusion. Signs: pain, pallor, blanching, skin hardness at IV site. Treatment: STOP infusion, leave catheter in place, inject phentolamine 5-10 mg diluted in 10-15 mL NS through catheter and around site. Time-sensitive: treat within 12h.

k: hydrocortisone — stress dosing / relative adrenal insufficiency
glucocorticoid + mineralocorticoid / stress-dose steroid / adrenal crisis treatment
chunks.x:
DRUG: Hydrocortisone — Stress Dosing / Relative Adrenal Insufficiency
Class: Glucocorticoid + mineralocorticoid / Stress-dose steroid / Adrenal crisis treatment
Category: antiinflam
Levels: pfc, ccatt
Primary use: Relative adrenal insufficiency in septic shock; adrenal crisis; stress dosing for surgical/trauma patients on chronic steroids; severe acute asthma; spinal cord injury
Mechanism: Hydrocortisone has both glucocorticoid AND mineralocorticoid activity (unlike methylprednisolone/dexamethasone which are pure glucocorticoids); cortisol replacement in adrenal insufficiency restores vasopressor responsiveness and hemodynamic stability; anti-inflammatory in severe asthma/allergic reactions; CRASH-2 equivalent for spinal cord injury methylprednisolone protocol controversial
WARNINGS: NOT for routine septic shock treatment (ADRENAL trial: no mortality benefit). Hyperglycemia — monitor glucose closely. Increased infection risk with prolonged high-dose steroids. Psychiatric effects (mania, psychosis). Taper required after prolonged use to prevent adrenal crisis on withdrawal.
Notes: Adrenal crisis pearls: (1) Think adrenal crisis in any patient with refractory hypotension on steroids or with pituitary/adrenal pathology. (2) Hydrocortisone (not dexamethasone) for adrenal crisis — need both glucocorticoid AND mineralocorticoid. (3) Give hydrocortisone first, test cortisol levels later.

k: somatostatin analogue / splanchnic vasoconstrictor / hormonal inhibitor
chunks.x:
DRUG: Octreotide (Sandostatin)
Class: Somatostatin analogue / Splanchnic vasoconstrictor / Hormonal inhibitor
Category: vasoactive
Levels: pfc, ccatt
Primary use: Variceal hemorrhage; sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycemia; carcinoid crisis; GI bleeding adjunct; post-ERCP pancreatitis prevention
Mechanism: Somatostatin analogue → activates somatostatin receptors (SSTR2/5) → inhibits splanchnic vasodilation → reduces portal pressure → controls variceal bleeding; also inhibits insulin, glucagon, GH, VIP, gastrin, secretin → reduces rebound hypoglycemia in sulfonylurea OD; anti-motility effects for severe diarrhea
WARNINGS: Hyperglycemia or hypoglycemia possible (complex hormonal effects — monitor glucose). Cholelithiasis with long-term use. Bradycardia. QTc prolongation. GI side effects (nausea, abdominal cramping). Rapid IV administration may cause cardiac effects — give bolus slowly over 3 min.
Notes: Sulfonylurea OD teaching: dextrose alone is insufficient. Sulfonylurea OD requires octreotide to stop the insulin release that keeps causing hypoglycemia. Without octreotide, patient requires continuous dextrose infusion and ICU monitoring. With octreotide: glucose stabilizes and monitoring duration dramatically reduced.

DRUG: Cefadroxil (Duricef)
Class: 1st generation cephalosporin / Beta-lactam (oral)
Category: abx
Levels: r12, pfc, ccatt
Primary use: TCCC 2026 battlefield wound antibiotic (oral, preferred)
Mechanism: Binds penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs) → inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis → bactericidal; oral first-generation cephalosporin with good gram-positive (streptococci, MSSA) and moderate gram-negative coverage; long half-life enables once-daily dosing
WARNINGS: Penicillin allergy cross-reactivity (~1-2% true cross-reactivity with cephalosporins). Dose adjustment required in significant renal impairment. Not active against Pseudomonas or MRSA.
Notes: Added to TCCC-RX per TCCC Change 25-1, which made cefadroxil the preferred oral wound antibiotic, replacing moxifloxacin. Once-daily oral dosing is a logistic advantage in prolonged field care.

Cefadroxil (Duricef) — R12 context: TCCC 2026 oral wound antibiotic of choice: cefadroxil 1g PO once daily, for all open combat wounds and invasive procedures when the casualty can take PO meds. Also the oral option for penetrating eye trauma (1g PO). Replaced moxifloxacin (TCCC Change 25-1).
Cefadroxil (Duricef) — PFC context: TCCC 2026: 1g PO once daily — preferred oral antibiotic for open combat wounds. Once-daily dosing simplifies the prolonged field care medication schedule.
Cefadroxil (Duricef) — CCATT context: Oral step-down option once casualty tolerates PO. 1g PO once daily. Continue wound antibiotic coverage per TCCC Guidelines.

k: non-opioid analgesic / selective nav1.8 sodium channel inhibitor
chunks.x:
DRUG: Suzetrigine (Journavx)
Class: Non-opioid analgesic / Selective Nav1.8 sodium channel inhibitor
Category: analgesia
Levels: r12, pfc, ccatt
Primary use: TCCC 2026 Combat Wound Medication Pack (CWMP) analgesic; moderate-to-severe acute pain, non-opioid
Mechanism: Selective inhibitor of the Nav1.8 voltage-gated sodium channel, which is expressed in peripheral nociceptive neurons (dorsal root ganglion). Binds the voltage-sensing domain 2 with ~3,100-fold selectivity over other Nav channels, stabilizing the closed state → blocks pain-signal action potentials in the periphery before they reach the CNS. No CNS activity and no addictive potential.
WARNINGS: Avoid grapefruit (CYP3A interaction). Dose adjustment recommended in hepatic impairment and with concomitant moderate CYP3A inhibitors. Not studied beyond 14 days of use. Clinically significant QTc prolongation seen at 2x the maximum recommended exposure. Common adverse effects: itching, muscle spasms, increased creatine phosphokinase, rash.
Notes: Added to TCCC-RX per the TCCC 2026 CWMP update. Suzetrigine (Journavx, Vertex) received FDA approval on 30 January 2025 as the first non-opioid analgesic approved for moderate-to-severe acute pain. Its peripheral, non-addictive mechanism is the reason it fits the CWMP mission-capable profile.

k: non-opioid analgesic / selective nav1.8 sodium channel inhibitor
chunks.x: Suzetrigine (Journavx) — R12 context: TCCC 2026 CWMP component for a casualty who can stay in the fight / mission-capable. Non-opioid — no respiratory depression, no sedation, no addictive potential, so it does not compromise airway, mentation, or security posture.

k: dissociative anesthetic / nmda antagonist (s-enantiomer of ketamine)
chunks.x:
DRUG: Esketamine
Class: Dissociative anesthetic / NMDA antagonist (S-enantiomer of ketamine)
Category: analgesia
Levels: r12, pfc, ccatt
Primary use: TCCC 2026 analgesia option for the non-mission-capable casualty; intranasal dissociative analgesia
Mechanism: S-enantiomer of ketamine; non-competitive NMDA receptor antagonism → dissociative analgesia. Higher NMDA-receptor affinity than the racemic mixture, allowing comparable analgesia at lower total dose. Intranasal route avoids the need for IV access.
WARNINGS: Co-administration of benzodiazepines with esketamine is NOT recommended (TCCC 2026). Monitor airway, breathing, and circulation closely. Disarm and consider disconnecting communications equipment for casualties given dissociative analgesics. If a casualty appears partially dissociated, TCCC 2026 advises it is safer to give more esketamine/ketamine than to add a benzodiazepine. TBI and/or eye injury does not preclude use, but use caution as sedation may obscure the neurologic exam.
Notes: Added to TCCC-RX per the TCCC 2026 analgesia update, which lists esketamine 14 or 28mg IN as an option alongside ketamine for the non-mission-capable casualty. As the S-enantiomer of ketamine, it offers comparable dissociative analgesia at a lower total dose.

Listed alongside ketamine (100mg IM / 50mg IN / 25mg IV-IO). Intranasal — no IV access required.

k: antioxidant / free radical scavenger / endothelial protectant (high-dose parenteral)
chunks.x:
DRUG: High-Dose IV Vitamin C (Ascorbic Acid)
Class: Antioxidant / Free radical scavenger / Endothelial protectant (high-dose parenteral)
Category: antiinflam
Levels: ccatt
Primary use: Burn resuscitation adjunct — fluid requirement reduction; investigational antioxidant resuscitation
Mechanism: At high parenteral doses, ascorbic acid is a potent scavenger of oxygen free radicals in the endothelium → limits postburn lipid peroxidation and microvascular protein/fluid leakage → reduces resuscitation fluid requirements and edema. Distinct in concept from low-dose micronutrient vitamin C (see note): this is a pharmacologic antioxidant resuscitation strategy, not nutritional repletion.
WARNINGS: Oxalate is a metabolite of ascorbic acid — high-dose IV vitamin C carries a risk of acute kidney injury and oxalate nephropathy; monitor renal function and avoid in established renal failure. Can cause hemolysis in G6PD deficiency — screen before high-dose use. Can cause false readings on point-of-care glucose meters. The burn-resuscitation use is an adjunct only and is investigational/emerging; it is not TCCC-endorsed and does not replace the TCCC 2026 USAISR Rule of Ten crystalloid resuscitation.
Notes: Created as a separate entry from the low-dose micronutrient vitamin C (zinc_vitC, electrolyte category): although the same molecule, high-dose IV antioxidant resuscitation and low-dose nutritional repletion are clinically distinct concepts with different doses, routes, indications, and risks. Mechanistic dual-use example: a single free-radical-scavenging / endothelial-protection mechanism connects burn fluid-sparing to investigational use in septic shock and ischemia-reperfusion injury. The burn indication is the best-supported (moderate); the others are tiered emerging/investigational and src-tagged.

k: antioxidant / free radical scavenger / endothelial protectant (high-dose parenteral)
chunks.x: High-Dose IV Vitamin C (Ascorbic Acid) — CCATT context: Burn resuscitation adjunct: high-dose IV ascorbic acid (commonly 66 mg/kg/hr IV during the first 24 h, per USAISR/Parkland-lineage protocols) reduces fluid requirements and edema in severe burns. Requires infusion capability and renal monitoring. An investigational antioxidant adjunct in sepsis and ischemia-reperfusion injury — evidence mixed. NOT a TCCC recommendation; TCCC 2026 burn resuscitation uses the USAISR Rule of Ten with crystalloid.

k: severe burn resuscitation — fluid requirement reduction
antioxidant / free radical scavenger / endothelial protectant (high-dose parenteral)
chunks.x:
High-Dose IV Vitamin C (Ascorbic Acid) for Severe burn resuscitation — fluid requirement reduction
Best-supported high-dose use. 66 mg/kg/hr IV during the first 24 h (originating from a randomized prospective study, JAMA Surgery 2000) attenuates postburn lipid peroxidation, reduces resuscitation fluid volume, body weight gain, and wound edema, and may improve gas exchange and renal function. A large multicenter RCT (VICToRY) using 50 mg/kg q6h × 96 h is evaluating organ dysfunction and survival. Adjunct to — not a replacement for — the TCCC 2026 USAISR Rule of Ten crystalloid resuscitation.
chunks.u: Severe burn resuscitation — fluid requirement reduction

k: antioxidant / free radical scavenger / endothelial protectant (high-dose parenteral)
chunks.x:
High-Dose IV Vitamin C (Ascorbic Acid) for Septic shock — antioxidant / vasopressor-sparing adjunct
Mechanistic dual use: free-radical scavenging and endothelial protection target the oxidative-inflammatory component of septic vasoplegia. Some studies (including burn-sepsis case-control data) report reduced fluid balance and norepinephrine requirements; the CITRIS-ALI RCT in sepsis with ARDS had mixed results. Evidence is inconsistent — emerging-grade.

k: antioxidant / free radical scavenger / endothelial protectant (high-dose parenteral)
chunks.x:
High-Dose IV Vitamin C (Ascorbic Acid) for Ischemia-reperfusion injury — endothelial free-radical scavenging
Mechanistic rationale: the reperfusion oxidative burst damages endothelium; high-dose ascorbate scavenges free radicals and may limit reperfusion injury. Direct clinical trauma evidence is limited — rationale-grade, listed for mechanistic completeness.

k: respiratory fluoroquinolone / dna gyrase / topoisomerase iv inhibitor
chunks.x:
DRUG: Moxifloxacin
Class: Respiratory fluoroquinolone / DNA gyrase / Topoisomerase IV inhibitor
Category: abx
Levels: r12, pfc, ccatt
Primary use: TCCC Tactical Field Care combat-wound antibiotic when casualty can take PO meds; 400 mg PO once daily (from the Combat Wound Medication Pack)
Mechanism: Inhibits bacterial DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV → bactericidal; broad gram-positive (streptococci including S. pneumoniae, MSSA), gram-negative, anaerobic, and atypical coverage; ~90% oral bioavailability — PO is effective without IV access
WARNINGS: QT prolongation — avoid with other QT-prolonging drugs (Class IA/III antiarrhythmics, macrolides, antipsychotics) and in casualties with arrhythmias, hypokalemia, or myocardial ischemia. Tendon rupture/tendinitis (especially Achilles; risk increased with corticosteroids). Exacerbates myasthenia gravis. CNS effects: dizziness, headache, peripheral neuropathy. C. difficile-associated diarrhea. Fluoroquinolone hypersensitivity; hepatic insufficiency per TCCC card.
Notes: TCCC recommends antibiotics for ALL open combat wounds — give early; wound infections can kill or delay recovery. Not reliable against MRSA or Pseudomonas aeruginosa — do not assume coverage. If the casualty later cannot take PO, transition to a parenteral agent per TCCC/medical direction; when stepping back down to PO, begin moxifloxacin immediately after the final parenteral dose for antibiotic overlap.

k: carbapenem / 1-beta-methyl beta-lactam / cell wall synthesis inhibitor
chunks.x:
DRUG: Ertapenem (Invanz)
Class: Carbapenem (1-β-methyl) / Beta-lactam — cell wall synthesis inhibitor
Category: abx
Levels: r12, pfc, ccatt
Primary use: TCCC combat-wound antibiotic when casualty CANNOT take PO (shock, unconsciousness); 1 g IV/IO/IM once daily
Mechanism: Binds penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs) → inhibits cell wall synthesis → bactericidal; broad gram-positive, gram-negative, and anaerobic coverage; long half-life with high protein binding allows once-daily dosing. NO reliable coverage of Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Acinetobacter baumannii, or MRSA.
WARNINGS: Hypersensitivity to ertapenem/carbapenems or anaphylactic reaction to any beta-lactam. IM route is reconstituted with lidocaine HCl — contraindicated with amide local-anesthetic (lidocaine) hypersensitivity. Seizures and other CNS adverse effects reported — risk increased with renal impairment, CNS disorders, or excessive dose; dose-adjust in renal impairment (CrCl ≤30 mL/min: 500 mg daily). Reduces valproic acid levels (breakthrough seizure risk). C. difficile-associated diarrhea. Do not mix or co-infuse with dextrose-containing solutions; IV infuse over 30 minutes.
Notes: TCCC guidelines (through 2024) list ertapenem as the parenteral combat-wound antibiotic; guidance has varied across TCCC updates (ceftriaxone vs ertapenem) — verify current unit SOP and medical direction before use. Transition IV/IO to PO (e.g., moxifloxacin) as soon as the casualty can take PO to conserve supplies and equipment.
